bottomLine: Trouble is not God’s verdict on you. It is a testing ground, and God is working in it to make you whole, lacking in nothing. When you do not know what to do, ask Him. He gives to all liberally and without reproach, because the reproach your record deserved already fell on Christ. Ask Him alone. Close the back door. Count the trial as His work, and let Him finish it.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see who stands on the other side of your asking. He is not a foreman keeping score on a clipboard. He is not a father who made you pay for every question. He is not a judge waiting for you to slip. He is the God who gives — who gives to all, who gives liberally, who gives without one word of reproach, and who has promised in plain words that the man who asks will be given wisdom.

The dust told you that trouble meant God had turned away. But listen to who is telling you otherwise. James once did not believe in his own brother. Then that brother came out of the grave and appeared to him. Now he writes to scattered, pressed, poor believers, and the first thing he tells them is to count it all joy. He does not write from ease. He writes as a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, who rose and came to find him. If Christ could turn a doubting brother into a servant who wrote these words, He can work in this trial too. He has not lost the thread of yours.

So look at where the reproach went. It did not stay on your record, waiting for the day you finally ask. It fell on Jesus. The robbers on the crosses beside Him threw it at Him. The crowd threw it at Him. He took it without answering, and He bore it all the way into death so that the Father could open His hand to you with nothing held back. That is why you can ask today without bracing for the blow. The lecture you fear was spent on Christ.

And when your faith shakes and the wind pushes you around like a wave, remember the hand. Jesus did not wait for Peter to steady himself before He reached. He stretched out his hand, took hold of him. That same hand bears the nail mark now, and it is holding you. Ask Him for the wisdom you need this week. He will not throw your past in your face. He will give. He said so: it will be given to him. And this trial will not have the last word. The One who began the work in you will finish it.
closingVerse: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
carry: Where have you been grinding through a trial alone because you expected God to answer your asking with a lecture — when He has promised to give wisdom liberally and without reproach?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man keeps a line ready for the day he falls. It was a long week. She started it. The guys at work all talk that way. Nobody could have held out carrying what I was carrying. The oldest version is the first thing a man ever said after a sin: The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it. Adam blamed his wife — and through her, the God who gave her to him.

The dust still talks that way. It tells you the pull you feel is not really yours. God built you like this. God put the trouble in your path. God set the trap and then watched you walk into it. And if the bad things come from Him, the dust whispers, then the good things are uncertain — handed out by a God whose mood shifts like the light across a kitchen floor as the day wears on.

A man who believes that will blame God for his falls and doubt Him in his blessings, and he ends up face-down either way. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word of James 1:9–18 cuts both lies at the root. God tempts no one. Every good gift comes down from a Father who does not change. And the God who does not change has done the one thing sin can never do. He has given you birth, by His word, of His own will.

sections.heading: Two Trials, Two Births
pulls: The dust says God set the trap and then watched you walk into it. James says God tempts no one. Every good gift comes down from a Father who does not change — and He gave you birth on purpose.
paras: James has just told you to count your trials as joy and to ask God for wisdom in them. Now he names two trials most men never think of as trials at all: having little and having much. The poor brother is tempted to think he counts for nothing. The rich man is tempted to think his money makes him something. Both are tested by what is in the bank, and both need to see where they stand before God. The test is what you lean on.

Then James draws a hard line between a trial and a temptation. God sends trials to prove a man and grow him. He never sends the pull toward sin; that rises from inside. And at the center of the passage stand two births set against each other. Desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin grows up into death. God, of His own will, gives birth to sons by the word of truth. Everything this week turns on which birth you belong to. Read the ten verses through twice before you go on, and watch for the moment the passage turns from what you do to what God has done.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE LOW PLACE AND THE HIGH
paras: James starts with money, because money is one of the first places a man is tested. But let the brother in humble circumstances glory in his high position. The man with the thin paycheck, the old truck, the second job on Saturdays — James calls him brother and tells him to boast. Not in what he lacks. In where God has set him. He has been brought into the family of God and made an heir of a kingdom (James 2:5). No bank statement can lower that.

Then James turns to the other man: and the rich, in that he is made humble, because like the flower in the grass, he will pass away. The rich man is told to boast in being brought low. That sounds like nonsense until you see what is coming. For the sun arises with the scorching wind and withers the grass. A field that is green in May is straw by August. The wealth, the title, the land with his name on the gate — So the rich man will also fade away in his pursuits. He fades in the middle of the work, before he ever gets to retire.

Poverty and plenty are both trials, and God uses both to finish His work in a man. Both men stand on the same ground, and that ground is grace. Christ is the measure of it: though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich. The poor man is rich because Christ made him so. The rich man is safe only when he has been made low enough to need the same Christ. Whichever man you are this week, your boast is the same. It is not what you have. It is who has you.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE CROWN AND THE BLAME
paras: James gathers the trials back up and attaches a promise: Blessed is a person who endures temptation, for when he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord promised to those who love him. Look at the order. The crown is promised before the man ever walks into the trial. It is a gift held out, not a wage being earned. And it goes to those who love him — men who were loved first. Christ, who endured the cross, is the One holding it out: Be faithful to death, and I will give you the crown of life.

Then James shuts the oldest escape hatch a man has. You do not get to say God tempted you, for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. God sends trials. He tests a man the way a smith tests iron — to prove it and to make it stronger. But He never baits a man toward sin. The trial is His. The pull toward evil is not. A trial comes to make you stand. A temptation comes to make you fall.

This matters more than it looks. A man who blames God for his temptation has to keep God at arm’s length; you cannot run to the one you think set the trap. But a man who knows God tempts no one can run straight to Him in the middle of the fight. And he will find a Helper there who knows the fight from the inside. Christ has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin. He is the way out.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: BAIT, BIRTH, AND DEATH
pulls: Sin conceived in the dark grows up into death. But the Father of lights, of His own will, gave you birth by the word of truth — and what He has given birth to, He does not abandon.
paras: So where does the pull come from? James says it plainly: But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. The word for enticed is built on the word for bait. Nobody bites a bare hook. The bait is always something you already want — the screen at midnight, the second drink, the shortcut on the invoice, the comment that will put the other man in his place. The hook is hidden underneath. And the hunger that makes the bait work is yours.

Mark the line James draws. Being tempted is not the same as sinning; Christ was tempted in every way and never once sinned. But do not call your own lust innocent. James names it as the source, and when the will takes it in, it does what it was always going to do. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. Desire and the will come together, and something is conceived. It grows in the dark. And then it is born.

It does not stay small. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death. The lie that seemed small at lunch is a habit by Christmas and a broken house in five years. That is the end of the line for every sin left to grow: death, the wage it was always going to pay (Romans 6:23). But that verse does not stop at the wage: the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Christ took the death your sin was growing toward. And If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins. What was conceived in the dark can be dragged into the light and put to death at the cross.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: BORN BY HIS WILL
paras: Don’t be deceived, my beloved brothers. The deception James means is the one the dust has been telling all along: that God is the source of your evil and stingy with your good. James turns it over. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. Every one. The pay that covered the mortgage, the wife who stayed, the morning you woke up sober, the breath in your chest right now — all of it came down from Him.

And He does not shift. The Father made the sun and the moon and the stars, and every one of them moves; the shadow of the barn swings across the yard and stretches long by evening. But the Father of lights is One with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow. He is not kind in the morning and cold by dark. What He was toward you at the cross, He is toward you today.

Then James sets a second birth against the first. Lust conceived and gave birth to sin, and sin to death. But Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures. No one talked God into it. He willed it. He used the word of truth — the good news of a crucified and risen Christ — to bring you to life. And He made you first fruits, the first sheaf of a harvest still coming in. Christ heads that harvest: But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruits of those who are asleep. The life in you is the life that walked out of the tomb.

stations.verse: For the sun arises with the scorching wind and withers the grass, and the flower in it falls, and the beauty of its appearance perishes. So the rich man will also fade away in his pursuits.
stations.question: What am I counting on to make me somebody — the paycheck, the title, the land — that the heat of one hard season could wither?
stations.live: Write down the one possession or position you most count on to make you somebody. Beside it write: ‘This will fade.’ Under it write: ‘My inheritance in Christ will not.’ Keep the card where you see it.
body: Marainō first meant to quench a fire, and in the passive, of a fire dying down and going out. It came to mean to waste away, and later writers used it of flowers and grass withering in the heat. The Greek Old Testament uses it that way in Job. James 1:11 is its only appearance in the New Testament.

James puts it at the end of his sentence like a door swinging shut: So the rich man will also fade away in his pursuits. Not crushed. Faded, like a coal going grey while he is still bent over his work. Money does not hold its color, and neither does the man who leans on it.

The dust says what you own is what makes you last. But Peter uses a related word, with a negative attached, for what Christ has won for you: an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn’t fade away. Your holdings wither. His do not, and they are kept for you.

stations.verse: But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.
stations.question: What bait keeps working on me because of a hunger in me that I would rather blame on someone else?
stations.live: Name your bait — the thing that looks like food and hides a hook. Find the hour of day it usually shows up. Before that hour comes this week, pray: ‘Lord Jesus, You were tempted. Help me now.’
body: Deleazō comes from delear, bait. It means to lure with bait, and so to allure or entice. It appears three times in the New Testament — here, and twice in 2 Peter 2, where false teachers are enticing unsettled souls and where they entice in the lusts of the flesh.

Bait works because it looks like food. The trap hides under the thing you want. James says a man is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. The bait finds him because something in him is already hungry — for comfort, for control, for being noticed, for one more hour of not feeling anything.

The dust says you were set up. Deleazō says the bait worked on your own appetite. That is hard to hear, but it is good news too, because Christ knows exactly where to meet you. For in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.

stations.verse: Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.
stations.question: What desire have I been letting grow in the dark, as if it would stay small and never be born into something worse?
stations.gloss: to conceive; to take hold of
stations.live: Name the desire you have been feeding in private. Bring it into the light this week: tell God plainly, and tell one brother. Then say it out loud: ‘I will not let this come to term.’
body: Syllambanō means to take hold of. Its sixteen New Testament uses run wide — men seized as prisoners, fishermen taking a catch, a friend lending a hand, and a woman conceiving a child. James takes that last sense and makes it a picture of lust producing sin.

The same word marks both ends of Christ’s road to the cross. The angel told Mary, you will conceive in your womb and give birth to a son. And on the last night, the soldiers seized Jesus and bound him. Conceived for you. Seized for you. Handed over in your place.

The dust says the desire you are feeding is small and will stay that way. James says what is conceived will be born. But the Son who was conceived in Mary and seized in the garden went all the way to death, so that what your desire conceived would not have the last word over you.

stations.verse: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.
stations.question: Where do I treat God’s kindness toward me as a mood that might shift by tomorrow, instead of the gift of a Father who does not change?
stations.live: Each evening this week, name three good gifts from the day — small ones count. After each one, say: ‘From above. From the Father who does not change.’
body: Parallagē means change or variation — a thing shifting from one state to another. It appears only here in the New Testament. James sets it beside the turning of shadows, a picture any man who has worked outside from sunup to dark knows in his body. Nothing under the sky holds still for long.

Every light you have ever worked under moves. The sun climbs and drops. The moon thins and fills. The stars wheel over the back field all night. But the Father of lights has no variation, nor turning shadow. The Maker of every moving light does not move.

The dust says God’s favor is like weather — warm today, cold tomorrow, and you never know which until you step outside. Parallagē shuts that down. What God was toward you when Christ died for you, He is toward you this morning, and He will be the same when you lie down tonight. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.

stations.verse: Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures.
stations.question: How would I walk into this week if I believed my new birth was the settled will of a Father who meant to have me?
stations.live: When you wake this week, before your feet hit the floor, say: ‘Of His own will He gave me birth. He meant to have me.’ Then get up and go to work as a son.
body: Boulomai means to will or to purpose. It leans harder toward deliberate choice than the more common word for wanting, and the form James uses in 1:18 means of set purpose. It occurs thirty-seven times in the New Testament, often of a man settling what he will do.

It is the word in Jesus’ prayer in the garden: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. The Father willed the cup. The Son drank it to the bottom. Your new birth rests on that same will — purposed, settled, and carried through at the cross.

The dust says God was talked into you and could be talked out of you. Boulomai says He meant it. Of his own will he gave birth to us. Nothing you did started it, and nothing you do will make Him wish He had not. Hebrews uses the same word for God being determined to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel.

practices.title: BOAST IN THE RIGHT PLACE
practices.body: Whether money is tight or plenty this month, it is a trial God is using. If you are short, write down what you hold in Christ that no lender can touch: forgiven, adopted, an heir of the kingdom. If you have more than enough, write down what you would still have if it were all gone tomorrow. Both men boast in the same place — in Christ, who became poor to make you rich. Say that line aloud before you check the account.

practices.title: STOP BLAMING THE GIVER
practices.body: Listen for your excuses this week. It was a long day. She started it. Anyone would have done the same. Every one of them points the finger somewhere else, and the oldest ones point at God. James says he himself tempts no one. When you fall, say plainly what happened and own it. Then go straight to the Father, who does not tempt and does forgive. Christ has already opened the way home; owning it is how you walk back in.

practices.title: NAME THE BAIT AND THE HOUR
practices.body: Temptation keeps a schedule. Find yours. Write down what the bait is, what time of day it shows up, and what you are usually feeling when it does — tired, angry, lonely, bored. Then set one guard at that hour this week: the phone charges in the kitchen, you leave before the second round, you call a brother at nine. God has promised a way of escape with every temptation. Take it, even when it feels small.

practices.title: KILL IT BEFORE IT GROWS
practices.body: Sin left in the dark grows. James traces it from desire to conception to birth to death. Do not wait for it to come to term. This week, confess the thing you have been feeding — to God, and to one man you trust. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins. Christ already died for it. Bring it to Him while it is small, and let a brother help carry it.

practices.title: COUNT THE GIFTS COMING DOWN
practices.body: Every good gift comes down from the Father of lights. At supper this week, before you eat, name out loud one good gift from the day — the work that paid, the child who laughed, the rain on the field. Thank the Father for it by name. A man who sees every gift coming down from a Father who does not change will stop suspecting Him when the hard days come. Teach your children to do it with you.

title: The Father of Lights
subtitle: from dust to a birth by the word of truth
keyVerse: Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures.

passage.text: But let the brother in humble circumstances glory in his high position;
and the rich, in that he is made humble, because like the flower in the grass, he will pass away.
For the sun arises with the scorching wind and withers the grass, and the flower in it falls, and the beauty of its appearance perishes. So the rich man will also fade away in his pursuits.
Blessed is a person who endures temptation, for when he has been approved, he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord promised to those who love him.
Let no man say when he is tempted, “I am tempted by God,” for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.
But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.
Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.
Don’t be deceived, my beloved brothers.
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.
Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures.

stationsIntro: Take each verse one at a time and let it land before you answer. Where a Greek word is opened up, let it show you more plainly what God has done and what the dust has been hiding.
lifeIntro: God tempts no one, and every good thing on your table came down from Him. He gave you birth on purpose, by His word. So this week, put the blame where it belongs and the thanks where it is owed.
lifePulls: Two births run through this passage. Desire conceives sin, and sin grows into death. But the Father of lights, who does not change, has given you a new birth by His word — and He meant it.
prayer: Father of lights, every good gift I have came down from You. You do not change, and Your kindness toward me does not shift with the hours. Forgive me for blaming You for the pull I feel, when it rises from my own heart. Thank You that Jesus was tempted in every way and did not sin, and that He helps me when I am tempted. Show me the bait before I bite, and give me the way of escape You have promised. What I have let grow in the dark, I bring to You now. Put it to death at the cross. Whether I have little or much this week, let me boast only in Christ. Thank You that of Your own will You gave me birth by the word of truth. Keep me as a first fruit of Your harvest, for the glory of Your Son. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father of lights, every good gift I have came down from You.
You do not change, and Your kindness toward me does not shift with the hours.
Forgive me for blaming You for the pull I feel, when it rises from my own heart.
Thank You that Jesus was tempted in every way and did not sin, and that He helps me when I am tempted.
Show me the bait before I bite, and give me the way of escape You have
promised.
What I have let grow in the dark, I bring to You now. Put it to death at the cross.
Whether I have little or much this week, let me boast only in Christ.
Thank You that of Your own will You gave me birth by the word of truth.
Keep me as a first fruit of Your harvest, for the glory of Your Son.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: God tempts no one. The pull toward sin rises out of your own desire, and if you feed it, it will conceive, be born, and grow up into death. But God is not your problem. He is your Father. Every good gift comes down from Him, and He does not change. Of His own will He gave you birth by the word of truth. Own your sin. Credit Him with your gifts. Live as a son He meant to have.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the Father of lights. Every good gift you have came down from Him — the wages that came in on Friday, the rain on the field, the son who called. Every one was handed down by a Father who does not shift. Every one was meant. Every one is a word from Him that the bait, the excuses, and the bank balance cannot cancel. Look at the Maker of a sun that never stays still, the One with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.

The dust told you that God set the trap. But God tempts no one. The hunger was yours, and the bait was the world’s, and the hook was the devil’s. God was never the trapper. He is the One who came down into the trap after you. His Son was tempted in every way and did not sin. Then He let Himself be seized, bound, and nailed to a cross, and He took the death your sin had been growing toward. Then He walked out of the grave alive, and the trap lay broken behind Him.

So look at the two births. Your desire conceived sin, and sin was on its way to death. That was the line you were on. But God set a second birth against it. Of His own will — not because you asked well, not because you cleaned up first — He gave you birth by the word of truth. The good news of Jesus Christ crucified and risen got into you, and you were made alive. That birth will not be undone, because the will behind it does not change. A father does not unbirth a son. Your Father will not unbirth you.

And you are first fruits. The first sheaf off a field is the promise of the whole harvest. Christ came out of the grave as the first fruits of those who are asleep, and you belong to the harvest that follows Him. The crown of life is promised to those who love Him, and it is held out by the One who loved you first. Whatever is fading in your hands this week, this does not fade. Of His own will He gave you birth, and the Father of lights does not change His will. Stand up, son, and go out to the work as one born on purpose.
closingVerse: Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures.
carry: Where have you been blaming God, your wife, or your week for a pull that rose from your own desire, when the Father who gave you birth on purpose stands ready to forgive it?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: You have heard more sermons than you can count. You could pass a test on most of them. You know what the Bible says about anger, about your mouth, about the widow down the road whose gutters have hung loose since her husband died. You nodded at all of it, and some of it you underlined. And somewhere along the way you started to believe the nodding was the thing — that a man who agrees with the word has mostly done what it says.

That is the lie the dust tells about the word of God. It says the word is information, and a man who stores enough of it is safe. It says hearing is a kind of doing. So you walk out of the pew the same man who sat down in it. By Monday the temper is back, the side comment is back, the phone is back, and none of it feels like a contradiction, because you still agree with every verse.

Behind that lie stands a second one. When the gap between what you hear and what you do finally shows, the dust tells you the fix is grit. Clench your jaw. Try harder. White-knuckle the next week. Either way the word stays outside you, a sign nailed to the wall instead of a seed in the ground. Psalm 119:25 is the cry of a man who has found out that neither lie gives life: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

James answers that cry with a farmer’s word. The word of God is not posted over you. It is planted in you — the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. And seed God has put in the ground does not stay seed.

sections.heading: Ear, Tongue, and Hand
pulls: The dust says the word of God is information to store and agree with. James says it is seed the Father has already put in the ground of you — and seed God plants does not stay seed.
paras: This passage grows straight out of the verse before it. James has just said of the Father, Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth. Everything in verses 19 through 27 rests on that birth. The man James is talking to has already been made alive by a word he did not write and could never have spoken to himself. Now James shows what that word does once it is in him, and what it looks like when it comes up through a man’s life.

Watch how the passage moves down the body. It starts at the ear: swift to hear. It moves to the mouth and the temper: slow to speak, slow to anger. It stops at a mirror, goes back to a tongue that needs a bridle, and ends at the hands and feet that go out to the fatherless and the widow. James is tracing the path of one seed as it pushes up through the whole man. Read the nine verses aloud before you go on. Read them slowly, and listen.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: SWIFT TO HEAR
paras: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. Mark the So, then. James is drawing a line from the verse before it. God spoke first. He spoke you into new life by the word of truth, and you did not help. A man who was born by listening ought to stay a listener. Your ears are the first place the new birth shows.

Most men run it backward. Quick to speak, slow to hear, quick to anger. Your wife starts a sentence and you have the answer loaded before she reaches the verb. A man on the crew questions your numbers and the heat climbs your neck before he finishes. You call it being decisive. James calls it upside down.

Then he gives the reason: for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God. Your anger feels like it is on God’s side. It feels like justice with its sleeves rolled up. But it grows nothing God wants. It is gasoline thrown on a brush pile — a great deal of heat, and nothing planted when the smoke clears. Proverbs sets the two side by side: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

Look at Christ before the men who hated Him. When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. He had every right to anger and every word ready, and He committed himself to him who judges righteously. He did that in your place, and in Him you are counted righteous already. You do not need your temper to secure the righteousness of God. It was secured at the cross.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE WORD PLANTED DEEP
paras: Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness. James knows what grows in an untended field. Leave ground alone a season and it fills with whatever the wind carried in. The filth he names is not exotic. It is the joke you laughed at, the site you went back to, the grudge you water every night before you sleep. Overflowing of wickedness fits a heart that holds more than it can carry, and it spills.

But putting away is not the main verb. The main verb is receive. Receive with humility the implanted word. A man clears rocks and pulls weeds for one reason: to make room for seed. And the seed is already there. James calls it implanted. God put it in you when He gave you birth by the word of truth. You cannot make the word or force it up. Your work is to stop fighting it.

Humility here is the posture of soil. Soil does not argue with seed. It does not tell the farmer what crop it would rather grow. A proud man reads the Bible looking for a verse that agrees with him. A humble man takes it the way dry dirt takes rain.

And look at what the seed can do: which is able to save your souls. Not tidy them. Save them. The word planted in you carries the news of a Savior who was laid in the ground and came up out of it alive. Seed with that inside it does not rot in the dirt. The seed saves your soul. Your weeding never could.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE MAN AT THE MIRROR
pulls: The word that shows you your face is the word that has already set you free. A man made free does not stand at the mirror forever. He walks out the door and does what he saw.
paras: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves. The man who only hears is not standing still. He is fooling himself. His danger is not that he disagrees with the word. He agrees with all of it. His danger is that agreement has become his hiding place.

Then the picture. A man looks at his natural face in a mirror. He sees the stubble, the grey, the nick on his chin. Then he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was. You know that man. You have been him. A sermon holds up your face — the sharp word at supper, the money you keep from your wife, the silence when you ought to speak — and by the time you are halfway home it is gone.

Now the other man. But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues. He bends down and looks hard. He stays. James calls it a law of freedom, because the word that shows you your face is the word that has already set you free. Christ kept that law in your place. He was the one perfect doer, and He died for every hearer who forgot. You are not justified by your doing; a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law. But a man made free does not stand at the mirror forever.

This man will be blessed in what he does. The blessing is found in the doing, not paid out after it. Jesus said the man who hears these words of mine, and does them builds his house on a rock. The rain comes either way. What you hear and then do is where the house stands.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: RELIGION THAT VISITS
paras: If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless. James picks a word for the outward side of faith — the attending, the giving, the bowed head before meals. He does not mock it. He tests it. A man can keep every outward habit and still let his mouth run loose: the jab at his son, the story about the deacon, the curse at the truck that cut him off. That man has fooled his own heart.

Then James names the real thing. Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world. Two motions. One goes out toward the people no one is watching. The other keeps the world’s grime off your hands while you go.

Before you hear it as a chore, see it as a portrait. God is the One who visits. When Jesus met a funeral at the gate of Nain — a widow carrying out her only son — He touched the coffin and gave the boy back to his mother, and the crowd said, God has visited his people. You were fatherless once. Christ said to men like you, I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you. And He washes His people so He can present them not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing.

So go to the widow on your road. Take the boy with no father fishing. Cut the grass. Sit in the hospital room. Keep your heart out of the world’s mud, not to earn clean hands, but because Christ already washed them. A man God has visited goes visiting.

stations.verse: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.
stations.question: When the word of God cuts across what I already think, how quickly do I start arguing with it instead of listening?
stations.gloss: slow; dull to take something in
stations.live: Before you say one word about this week’s passage — to God, to your wife, to the men at your table — read James 1:18–21 aloud twice and write down one sentence it says to you. Then pray: ‘Lord, open the Scriptures to me. I am listening.’
body: Bradys means slow. It appears twice in the New Testament. Here James sets it against its opposite, tachys, quick: swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. The other time, the risen Christ says it on the Emmaus road: slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken.

That second use shows what James is after. The verse before says God gave birth to us by the word of truth. The verse after says receive with humility the implanted word. Swift to hear is more than letting your wife finish her sentence. It is how you take the word of God. A man can be slow to hear Scripture and quick to argue with it.

The dust says you already know what the Book says. Christ did not leave those two men slow. He explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself, and their hearts burned. He still opens the word to slow men.

stations.verse: Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
stations.question: Where do I keep the word of God on a shelf like advice for hard days, instead of receiving it as seed the Father has already planted in me?
stations.live: Pick one verse from this passage and say it aloud each morning before you look at anything else. Do not try to force it to grow. Give it ground: ‘Lord, I receive Your word with humility.’
body: Emphytos comes from a verb meaning to plant in. The New Testament uses it only here. The word can mean inborn — a thing a man carries in him from the start — or rooted, set into the ground by another hand. James means the second.

James takes the word and turns it around. Something has been set in the ground of you that goes deeper than the sin you were born with — the word of truth by which the Father gave you birth. It is not paint on the surface. It has roots, and roots go down where you cannot follow them — under the habits, under the temper, under the things you have never said out loud.

The dust says you were born this way and will die this way, and every relapse proves it. Emphytos says God has planted something in you deeper than your birth in Adam, and that word is able to save your souls.

stations.verse: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
stations.question: Where have I been calling my agreement with the word of God obedience, when I have only nodded at the right places?
stations.live: Take the last sermon you heard or the last passage you read. Write down one thing it told you to do. Do it before Saturday, and tell no one. Let the word, not the credit, be the point.
body: Poiētēs is built on poieō, to make or to do. In older Greek it meant a maker, and especially a poet; Paul uses it that way in Acts 17:28, of the Greeks’ own poets. Later it came to mean a doer. James uses it in four verses — a doer of the word, of the work, of the law.

Paul writes that the doers of the law will be justified, and then shows that no son of Adam is one (Romans 3:20). Only Christ did all of it. He is the true Doer, and in Him you are counted righteous by faith. James is not reopening that question. He is showing what a man made new does next.

The dust wants you to think hearing is half the job. Poiētēs says a word received becomes a thing made — built with your hands, in the week you actually live, at the job and the table where people can see it.

stations.verse: If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless.
stations.question: If a man watched only my mouth this week, and not my church attendance, what would he conclude about my religion?
stations.live: Name the one person who gets your worst words. Put a bridle on your tongue with him this week. Before you speak, say it to yourself: ‘Christ is in this room. Is this word fit for Him?’
body: Thrēskeia means religion in its outward side — worship you can see. Paul uses it of the Pharisees, the strictest sect of our religion. In Colossians 2:18 it names a false worshiping of the angels. The word is neither good nor bad in itself. It names the visible part.

James does not tell you to quit church or skip the blessing at supper. He tells you the visible part can be hollow. A man can keep every outward form and let his tongue run like a loose horse in a hayfield. That man’s religion is worthless, and he does not know it. The people at his table know it.

The dust says the outward show is enough to get by on. Thrēskeia says the outward show was always meant to be the husk around something alive. Christ did not die to make you more religious. He died to make you His.

stations.verse: Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.
stations.question: Who is the widow or fatherless child within a few miles of my house that I have meant to look in on and have not?
stations.gloss: to visit; to look in on with care
stations.live: Put a name and a day on the calendar. Go see a widow or a fatherless child this week — fix the latch, bring supper, sit and listen. Go because you were visited.
body: Episkeptomai means to look in on, to visit — especially the sick and the suffering. Jesus uses it of the sick and the prisoner in Matthew 25:36, and of the ones no one went to see. The Greek Old Testament uses it again and again for God Himself coming to help His people, as when Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said.

That is why Zechariah sang that God has visited and redeemed his people, and why the crowd at Nain, watching a widow’s son sit up in his coffin, said God has visited his people. In Christ, God came down the road to your door. He did not send word. He came.

The dust says you are too busy, that somebody at church surely handles that, that it is not your place. Episkeptomai says you were visited first. A man the Lord has looked in on goes and looks in on the widow.

practices.title: LET HER FINISH
practices.body: Pick the person you most often cut off — your wife, your son, the foreman. For one week, let every sentence they start reach its end before you say a word. Then wait a three-count. James says let every man be swift to hear, and a man who was given life by a word God spoke has every reason to listen. You will hear things you have been talking over for years. Listening is not losing.

practices.title: PULL ONE WEED
practices.body: Name the one piece of filth that has grown up in the field this year — the site, the show, the bottle you hide, the grudge you replay. Do not bargain with it, and do not give it one more week. Pull it this week: cancel it, delete it, pour it out, or say it aloud to a brother. You are not clearing ground to earn the seed. The seed is already in. You are making room for it to grow.

practices.title: STOOP AND STAY
practices.body: Read James 1:19–27 every morning this week, slowly, three times through, before the coffee is gone. After the last reading, write one line: what did this mirror show me about myself? Do not dress it up. Then write a second line: what did it show me about Christ? A man who looks into the perfect law of freedom and stays there long enough sees both his own face and the face of the Savior who set him free.

practices.title: DO ONE THING YOU HEARD
practices.body: Before Sunday comes around again, take one plain thing the word told you to do, and do it. Not three things. One. Small is fine. Make the call you have put off. Pay back what you owe. Tell your son you were wrong without adding a but. Christ was the perfect doer in your place, which is why you can act without fear of failing. This man will be blessed in what he does.

practices.title: GO VISIT
practices.body: Find the widow on your road or the boy whose father is gone. Go this week with something in your hands — a meal, a tool, an hour of your Saturday. Do not make it a program, and do not wait for a committee. Make it a visit. God visited you in His Son when you had nothing to give back. Going to the fatherless and the widow is how that visit keeps moving down the road.

title: The Mirror and the Seed
subtitle: from dust to the word planted deep
keyVerse: Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

passage.text: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.
If anyone among you thinks himself to be religious while he doesn’t bridle his tongue, but deceives his heart, this man’s religion is worthless.
Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly, out loud if you can, and let it sit before you answer. Where a Greek word is opened up, let it press the verse a little deeper into the ground.
lifeIntro: This week is not about trying harder to be a better listener. It is about letting the word God already planted in you take root and come up — in your ears, in your mouth, and in your hands.
lifePulls: Christ did not shout instructions at you from the far side of the field. He came down your road, stood at your door, and planted His word in you. What He planted, He means to bring up.
prayer: Father, You gave me birth by the word of truth before I ever asked for it. You planted Your word in me, and it is able to save my soul. Make me swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger, starting at my own table. Pull out the filth I have let grow, and give me a humble heart to receive what You have sown. When I look into Your word and see my own face, keep me from walking off and forgetting. Thank You that Christ did everything You commanded in my place, and that I stand clean in Him. Send my hands to the widow and the fatherless, the way You came to me. Keep me unstained by the world until Jesus comes. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You gave me birth by the word of truth before I ever asked for it.
You planted Your word in me, and it is able to save my soul.
Make me swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger, starting at my own table.
Pull out the filth I have let grow, and give me a humble heart to receive what You have sown.
When I look into Your word and see my own face, keep me from walking off and forgetting.
Thank You that Christ did everything You commanded in my place, and that I stand clean in Him.
Send my hands to the widow and the fatherless, the way You came to me.
Keep me unstained by the world until Jesus comes.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: God gave you birth by His word and planted that word in you, and it is able to save your soul. So listen before you talk. Let your anger cool before it speaks. Pull the weeds and receive the seed with humility. Do not look in the mirror and walk off. Bridle your tongue, go see the widow, and keep your hands clean. You are not earning the word. You are letting it grow.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the mirror where you keep catching yourself and walking away. Lift them off the temper you have not tamed, off the tongue that got loose again on Tuesday, off the widow you meant to visit back in the spring. Lift them off the grit you have been trying to grow a harvest with. Lift them to the Sower who went out to sow. He did not wait for good ground. He made it. He broke you open with the word of truth and set His seed in you, and He has not dug it back up.

The dust told you the word was a sign on the wall — something to agree with and walk past. But the word in you is not paint. It has roots. The God who spoke light into the dark spoke life into you, and what He plants He tends. He waters it on the days you forget it is there. He pulls what you let grow up around it. Rain comes down and does not go back up empty. Neither does His word.

So look at the One who did what you have failed to do. Christ heard the Father perfectly and did everything He heard. He was slow to anger when He had every right to it, and when He was cursed He did not curse back. He was the only man who never walked away from the mirror, the only man whose religion was pure all the way through. Then He was laid in the ground like a seed, and the ground could not hold Him. The other disciple stooped, looked in, and saw the linen lying there with no body in it. Because Christ rose, the word planted in you carries resurrection in it.

Go into this week as a man who has been visited. God came down the road to you in His Son when you were fatherless and filthy, and He did not leave you alone. He gave His word on it: I will not leave you orphans. I will come to you. Hold that on Tuesday, when your temper flares and the mirror shows you the same old face. The seed is still in the ground. The risen Lord is still tending it. And the word implanted in you is able to save your souls — yours too, all the way to harvest.
closingVerse: Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
carry: Where has the word of God shown you your own face this year, while you kept walking away from that mirror instead of letting the seed come up?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man walks into a room and takes a reading. You do it before you know you are doing it. The truck in the lot. The boots, clean or worn. The grip of the handshake. The watch. Who the pastor greets first. In five seconds you have decided who matters in the room and where you stand next to them. Nobody taught you to do it out loud. You learned it on the playground and at the sale barn and in every office where a man waited to be called back.

That reading comes from a lie the dust tells about worth. It says a man is worth what he has gathered — money, title, name, the kind of house and the kind of crew he runs. It says worth is a ranking, and every room is a set of scales. Under the lie sits fear. If worth is a ranking, then yours can drop, and the only way to feel safe is to keep somebody below you.

So you give the good seat to the man who might help you, and you let the man who smells like the street stand by the door. You do not call it sin. You call it being practical, or reading the room, or knowing how things work. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a man who has found out that the scales are dust and he is lying in them: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

James answers with a question that takes the scales out of your hands: Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom? God has already done His seating. He did it at the cross, and He did not check your clothes first.

sections.heading: Two Men at the Door
pulls: The dust says worth is a ranking and every room is a set of scales. God already did His seating at the cross, and He did not check your clothes before He gave you a place.
paras: James writes to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion, and when he pictures their gathering he uses the old word for it — synagogue. These are scattered believers meeting in a room. A man walks in with gold on his hand. Another walks in with grime on his clothes. James stands the two of them in the doorway and asks what the people inside will do. He does not tell you which man is the better man. He asks where you will put them.

The passage runs in four movements. First the scene at the door and the sin in it (2:1–4). Then God’s choice of the poor, and what the rich have done to the church (2:5–7). Then the royal law, and why one broken command breaks the whole law (2:8–11). Last, the law of freedom and the mercy that wins over judgment (2:12–13). James starts and finishes in the same place. The faith you hold is the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory, and the One who holds the glory has already been merciful to you.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE LORD OF GLORY
paras: My brothers, don’t hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with partiality. This is one of only two places James names Jesus Christ, and he names Him here as the One who carries the glory. That settles the room before anyone walks in. All the glory in the building belongs to one Man, and He is not wearing a gold ring. Any honor you hand out at the door is borrowed from Him, and He gives His honor to sinners for nothing.

Then the scene. For if a man with a gold ring, in fine clothing, comes into your synagogue, and a poor man in filthy clothing also comes in. The usher sees both. To the first: Sit here in a good place. To the second: Stand there, or Sit by my footstool. It takes ten seconds. Nobody in the room would have called it sin. James calls it two sins at once. Haven’t you shown partiality among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts? You have split yourself down the middle — saying with your mouth that Christ is the Lord of glory, saying with your seating chart that money is. And you have climbed onto a judge’s bench you were never given. You looked at a ring and a stain and passed sentence.

Bring it home. It is the man at work whose calls you return in an hour and the man whose calls you never return. It is the couple you have over for supper and the couple you never think of. It is the way your voice changes when the owner walks onto the job, and the way it changes back when the hired man asks a question.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: RICH IN FAITH
paras: Listen, my beloved brothers. James stops the scene and makes you look at God’s own choices. Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom which he promised to those who love him? God did not pick by the ring. He has a long habit of taking the man the room overlooks and making him an heir.

He did it most plainly in His Son. Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich. The Lord of glory was laid in a feeding trough. He had nowhere to lay his head. At the end they stripped Him, threw a robe on Him to mock Him, and pressed thorns onto His head. If you want to know where God seats the poor, look at where God seated Himself.

So the partial man is not only rude. He is out of step with God. But you have dishonored the poor man. James reminds them who was hauling them into court — not the poor man by the door, but the rich men they were bowing to. Don’t they blaspheme the honorable name by which you are called? The name over you is Christ’s. Fawn over the man who mocks that name and shove aside the man God chose, and your loyalties are upside down.

Here is the grace inside it. If God chose the poor, then He chose you, because in every way that counts you came to Him with nothing. Christ’s word to a church that thought itself rich fits you before grace found you: miserable, poor, blind, and naked. He made you an heir anyway.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE ROYAL LAW
pulls: The law is one chain, and you have broken it. Christ kept every link and then carried the weight of your breaking. Now the royal law is not your ladder to God. It is His life coming up in you.
paras: However, if you fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well. James calls it royal. It is the King’s law, and it rules over the rest. Jesus set it beside the first commandment and said the whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments. If you love the man by the door as you love yourself, you will not leave him standing.

But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors. Then James shuts every exit. For whoever keeps the whole law, and yet stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all. The law is not a stack of separate rules where you can score well on most. It is one chain. Break one link and the chain is broken, no matter how many links held.

For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not commit murder.” The same God spoke both. You may be clean of one and guilty of the other. You may never have touched another woman and still sit on a grudge so long it has a name. James means to take away the scales — the ones where you rank yourself above the other sinners in the room.

And with the scales gone, one Man is left standing. Christ kept the whole law and did not stumble at one point. He loved His neighbor as Himself all the way to the cross, and he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree. You are not guilty of all anymore. His keeping is counted to you, and His blood covers every link you broke.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: MERCY TRIUMPHS
paras: So speak and so do, as men who are to be judged by a law of freedom. James turns your mouth and your hands toward the day of judgment. You will stand before God. But the law you will be measured by is a law of freedom — the law of a King who has already set you free and is writing His own love into you.

Then the hard sentence: For judgment is without mercy to him who has shown no mercy. A man who keeps a ledger on everyone else, who has no mercy for the poor man or the brother who wronged him, shows he has never seen his own debt. Mercy has never reached him, so he has none to give. James is not telling you to buy mercy with mercy. He is telling you that mercy received always leaks out of a man.

And then the last line, the one to carry all week: Mercy triumphs over judgment. At the cross, judgment and mercy met in one place, on one Man. The judgment was real. It fell on Christ in full, and nothing was waved off. Then God raised Him from the dead, and the judgment that had stood against you was spent. Because of the cross, the last word over you is mercy.

So be merciful at the door. Give the good seat away. Let the man who wronged you off the hook you have kept him on. Go easy on the brother who fell where you once fell. A man who knows the Judge has already spoken mercy over him has nothing left to guard and nobody left to rank.

stations.verse: For if a man with a gold ring, in fine clothing, comes into your synagogue, and a poor man in filthy clothing also comes in.
stations.question: Whose ring, truck, or title has quietly decided how warmly I treat a man before he has said a single word to me?
stations.live: Next time you walk into church, find the person dressed the worst or sitting alone and go to him first. Learn his name. Say it under your breath as you cross the room: ‘Christ is the only glory in here.’
body: Chrysodaktylios is one word: gold-ringed. It shows up nowhere else in the New Testament. James did not need a sentence to describe the man. One word did it. The room knew him by his hand before it knew his name, and that was all it cared to know.

That is what partiality does to a man. It shrinks him down to the thing he wears. The rich man becomes a ring. The poor man becomes a stain. Neither one is seen as a soul. And the people doing the seeing shrink too. They become a crowd that can be bought with a little gold.

The dust wants you to be known by what is on your hand. God marks His people by what was driven through His Son’s hands. Those wounds are the only thing that sets your place in His house, and they were paid for in blood, not worn for show.

stations.verse: Haven’t you shown partiality among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?
stations.question: Where have I been divided in myself, confessing Christ as the Lord of glory with my mouth while my choices say money and standing are what count?
stations.gloss: to divide; to make distinctions; to waver
stations.live: Name the one kind of man you quietly rank below you — the addict, the man on public help, the man with the accent. Pray for one of them by name this week: ‘You made no distinction, Lord. Neither will I.’
body: Diakrinō means to separate or sort — to make distinctions, to judge between. It can also mean to be divided in your own mind, to waver. James used it in 1:6 of the man who asks God and doubts. In 2:4 the word cuts both ways: the man sorts the room, and in sorting it he is split in two.

That is the trouble with favoritism. The man at the door is not just unkind. He has two faiths running at once — one that says Christ is the Lord of glory and one that says the gold ring is. He cannot carry both without being torn down the middle, and the tear shows every time someone new walks in.

The dust says sorting people is just good sense. But look at what God did: He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith. He did not sort you. He washed you. A man God refused to sort has no business sorting other men.

stations.verse: But you have dishonored the poor man. Don’t the rich oppress you, and personally drag you before the courts?
stations.question: Have I been bowing to people who use their power to press others down, because their favor might help me get ahead?
stations.gloss: to oppress; to lord it over
stations.live: Think of one place at work or at home where you hold power over someone else. Use it this week to lift a weight off him, not to press down: ‘Lord, make me strong the way You are strong.’
body: Katadynasteuō means to use power over someone — to oppress, to hold a man down. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Micah 2:2 of men who seize fields and houses by force. Picture a strong man’s boot on a weaker man’s neck. The New Testament uses it only twice.

Once here, of the rich who drag believers into court. The other time is Acts 10:38, where Peter says Jesus went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil. Same word. Men were held down, and Jesus came and lifted the weight off them with His own hands.

The dust says power is how a man stays safe, and you had better stand close to whoever has it. Christ shows you what power is for. He held all of it, and He spent it breaking the grip of the one who held you down. That is the only strength worth standing near.

stations.verse: However, if you fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well.
stations.question: Where am I treating love for my neighbor as one good habit among many, instead of the King’s own law that sets the terms for the rest of my life?
stations.live: Choose one neighbor — the man next door, or the one you find hardest to love. Do one thing for him this week you would want done for you. Say it as you go: ‘This is the King’s law.’
body: Basilikos means royal, belonging to a king. Luke uses it of Herod, who dressed himself in royal clothing. John uses it of a king’s man, a nobleman whose son lay sick at Capernaum. Set beside a law, it can mean a law made by the King, or a law that rules over the other laws. Both fit here.

Look at those two men. Herod wore the royal clothes, took the glory for himself, and was struck down. The nobleman came to Jesus and begged, Sir, come down before my child dies. The royal man who bowed was the one who went home with his son alive.

The dust says you can keep most of the law and skip the part about the man by the door. Basilikos says love of neighbor is the King’s law, and the King kept it first. He loved you as Himself, and He did it on a cross, wearing a crown of thorns instead of a ring of gold.

stations.verse: For judgment is without mercy to him who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
stations.question: Am I holding a man under a judgment I refuse to lift, while I stand every day under a mercy I did nothing to earn?
stations.gloss: to triumph over; to boast against
stations.live: Name the man you have been holding a judgment against. Do not wait to feel it. This week, speak one word of mercy to him or about him, and say to God: ‘Mercy won over me. Let it win here too.’
body: Katakauchaomai means to boast against, to exult over. It is a winner’s word. Paul uses it in Romans 11:18, telling Gentile believers, don’t boast over the branches. James will use it again in 3:14 of a proud and bitter heart. Here in 2:13 it is mercy that does the exulting.

That is a strange picture until you stand at the cross. Judgment came down on Christ in full. Nothing was waved off or marked down. The Father did not look away from sin; He laid it on His Son. And the grave gave Him back, and the judgment that had stood over you had nothing left to say. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

The dust says judgment always gets the final word. Katakauchaomai says mercy has the right to exult, and it exults over your record — every line of it. A man standing under that mercy can put down the ledger he keeps on his brother.

practices.title: GIVE UP YOUR SEAT
practices.body: This Sunday, find the person sitting alone or standing near the back — the one nobody is talking to. Go to him first, before you find your friends. Sit with him, even if it means leaving your usual pew. Learn his name and one thing about his week, and remember it next Sunday. Christ came all the way down to where you were and gave you a place in His house. This is how that place gets passed on.

practices.title: CATCH YOUR FIRST FIVE SECONDS
practices.body: For one week, notice the reading you take when a man walks in — the watch, the boots, the title. Catch it, and name it to yourself plainly. Then say under your breath, Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world? Let the verse correct the reading. You are not pretending not to see the difference. You are refusing to let it decide where a man belongs, because it did not decide where you belong.

practices.title: NAME THE ONE POINT
practices.body: Write down the one command you have quietly decided does not apply to you — the grudge you keep, the gossip you pass on, the man you look down on. James says whoever keeps the whole law, and yet stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all. Bring it to Christ, who kept every point in your place, and confess it plainly, out loud, by name. Then stop guarding it.

practices.title: USE YOUR WEIGHT TO LIFT
practices.body: Name the place where you have power over another person: an employee, a renter, a son, a man who owes you. This week, use that power the way Christ used His — to lift a load, not to press down. Forgive a debt. Give the day off when it costs you something. Pay what is fair before you are asked. Jesus went about healing all who were oppressed by the devil. Follow where He walked.

practices.title: LET MERCY WIN ONE FIGHT
practices.body: Pick one judgment you have been holding — against a brother, an old boss, your father. You do not have to pretend the wrong never happened. Christ did not pretend about yours; He bore it. But this week, let mercy have the last word. Pray for that man by name every morning, and ask God to do him good. If you can, do him some good yourself. Mercy triumphs over judgment, and it triumphed over you first.

title: The Good Seat
subtitle: from dust to the mercy that triumphs
keyVerse: Listen, my beloved brothers. Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom which he promised to those who love him?

passage.text: My brothers, don’t hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with partiality.
For if a man with a gold ring, in fine clothing, comes into your synagogue, and a poor man in filthy clothing also comes in,
and you pay special attention to him who wears the fine clothing and say, “Sit here in a good place;” and you tell the poor man, “Stand there,” or “Sit by my footstool”
haven’t you shown partiality among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?
Listen, my beloved brothers. Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom which he promised to those who love him?
But you have dishonored the poor man. Don’t the rich oppress you, and personally drag you before the courts?
Don’t they blaspheme the honorable name by which you are called?
However, if you fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well.
But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.
For whoever keeps the whole law, and yet stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all.
For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not commit murder.” Now if you do not commit adultery, but murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.

stationsIntro: Take each verse slowly and let it find the room you sat in last Sunday. Where a Greek word is opened up, let it show you the seat God gave you before you answer.
lifeIntro: God gave you a seat at His table when you came to Him with nothing, and Christ took the lowest place to make room for you. These practices carry that mercy out to the man by the door, the man under your hand, and the man you have been holding a judgment against.
lifePulls: Christ took the lowest seat in the house so that you could be given a place at His table. A man who has been seated by grace has no reason to guard the good chairs.
prayer: Father, You chose me when I came to You poor, blind, and naked. You did not look at my clothes or my record before You gave me a place in Your house. Forgive me for the way I size up men at the door and hand out the good seats. Forgive me for the one point of Your law I keep pretending does not apply to me. Thank You that Christ kept the royal law in full, and bore my breaking of it on the cross. Make me merciful the way You have been merciful to me. Let me use whatever strength I have to lift others, the way Jesus did. Teach me to see every man who walks through the door as one You might have chosen. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You chose me when I came to You poor, blind, and naked.
You did not look at my clothes or my record before You gave me a place in Your house.
Forgive me for the way I size up men at the door and hand out the good seats.
Forgive me for the one point of Your law I keep pretending does not apply to me.
Thank You that Christ kept the royal law in full, and bore my breaking of it on the cross.
Make me merciful the way You have been merciful to me.
Let me use whatever strength I have to lift others, the way Jesus did.
Teach me to see every man who walks through the door as one You might have chosen.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: The faith you hold belongs to the Lord of glory, and He did not check your clothes before He chose you. God picks the poor of this world and makes them heirs. So stop sizing men up at the door. Partiality is sin, and one broken point breaks the whole law. Christ kept it all and bore your breaking. Mercy has triumphed over judgment for you. Go and let it win again.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the Lord of glory standing in the doorway. He has seen every room you ever sized up. He has seen the men you bowed to and the men you looked past. He has seen the seat you were handed and the seat you were afraid of losing. And He is the Man who had the right to the best place in heaven and took the lowest place on earth, who did not ask what you were wearing when He made room for you.

The dust told you that worth is a ranking, and that the only safe man is the man with someone beneath him. But God has done His seating already. He chose the poor of this world to be rich in faith. He looked at you in your filthy clothes — the sin you could not scrub out, the record you could not hide — and He did not say Stand there. He brought you in, gave you a name that is not yours by birth, and made you an heir of the Kingdom He promised to those who love Him. You did not earn the chair. It was pulled out for you.

Look at what it cost Him. Christ kept the royal law at every point. He loved His neighbor as Himself, and He loved His enemies further than that. Then He stood under the judgment you had earned for every point you broke. It fell on Him without mercy, so that none of its weight would fall on you. It is finished, He said. Then He was raised from the dead, and now He is at the right hand of God, and He makes intercession for you.

So hold this on Tuesday, when the old reading comes back and you catch yourself ranking the room: Mercy triumphs over judgment. It is not a mood God is in. It is what happened at the cross, and it is the verdict the risen Christ is speaking over you right now. And when He comes again in glory, the poor man He chose will not be standing by the footstool. He will be seated at the King’s table — and so will you.
closingVerse: Listen, my beloved brothers. Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the Kingdom which he promised to those who love him?
carry: Who is the man you have quietly left standing by the door, and what would change if you saw him the way God saw you when He gave you a seat you had not earned?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: A man can say the right words for forty years. He can recite the creed, sing the old hymns without the book, and give the right answer when the preacher asks who Jesus is. And he can do all of it while his wife waits a month for one kind word, while the man two pews over loses his job and hears nothing from him but a promise to pray. The dust tells you that saying is the same as having. Say it once, sign the card, raise the hand, and you are covered — whatever the years after look like. Nobody ever has to see a thing.

The dust tells a second lie, and it is the mirror of the first. It says that because faith must show, it must be earned — that your standing with God climbs with every good deed and drops with every cold one. That lie sends a man to the kitchen table before dawn to tally his week like a timecard. The first lie lets you sleep in a dead faith. The second works you to death trying to keep a living one alive.

Both lies leave a man face-down, and Psalm 119:25 is his prayer: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word of James 2 is this. God does not save you by your works. He saves you by grace, through faith, in Christ alone — and the faith He gives is never a dead thing. It breathes. James wants you to know the difference between a corpse and a living man, and he wants you to know which one Christ has made you.

sections.heading: Paul and James at the Same Table
pulls: Faith alone joins you to Christ. But the faith that joins you to Christ is never alone. It breathes, and like breath on a cold morning, it can be seen.
paras: James, the Lord’s brother, writes to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion — believers scattered and pressed, some poor, some tempted to give the good seat to the man with the gold ring. He has just told them that Mercy triumphs over judgment. Now he asks what kind of faith a man has if mercy never travels from his mouth to his hands.

Read this passage beside Romans 3:28 — a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law — and some men decide the Bible is arguing with itself. It is not. Paul faces a man who wants to add his works to the cross as payment. James faces a man who wants to strip the life out of faith and keep the label. Paul says the root is faith alone. James says the root, if it is alive, bears fruit. Both are true, and you need both on the same morning. Paul says it himself in four words: faith working through love. The man leaning on his works needs Paul to kick the crutch away. The man leaning on his words needs James to ask him where his hands have been.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: SAYING IS NOT HAVING
paras: James opens with a question: What good is it, my brothers, if a man says he has faith, but has no works? Watch the verb. He does not say the man has faith. He says the man says he has faith. James is not weighing a real faith and finding it light. He is looking at a claim with nothing under it. Can faith save him? That kind — the kind that only talks — cannot.

Then he puts a body in front of you. If a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food, and you send them off with a blessing — Go in peace. Be warmed and filled — and keep your coat and your groceries, what good is it? The words are not wrong. Peace is a good word. Warmth is a good word. But words that cost you nothing and fill no stomach are breath on a window. They are gone before the man reaches the end of your drive.

Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself. Not weak. Not young. Dead. A dead thing can be dressed and laid out, but it does not move. It does not get up when a brother knocks at the door in the cold.

Before you hear that as a whip, hear what it assumes. James assumes real faith is alive because God made it alive. Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth (1:18). What God births breathes. Nobody has to teach a newborn to take his first breath. The question is not whether you can make your faith move by effort. It is whether the faith you hold is the one He gave.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: EVEN THE DEMONS BELIEVE
paras: Someone pushes back: You have faith, and I have works. As if faith and works were two kinds of Christian, two departments, and a man could pick the one that suits him. James will not have it. Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works. Faith lives in the heart, where only God reads. But it does not stay hidden. It comes out through the hands the way heat comes out of a woodstove. You have never seen the wind either. You have seen the trees bend.

Then the hard sentence. You believe that God is one. You do well. That is Israel’s confession from Deuteronomy 6:4, and James says it is right to believe it. The demons also believe, and shudder. The demons are not confused about God. When Jesus walked into the synagogue at Capernaum, an unclean spirit named Him on sight: I know you who you are: the Holy One of God. What they lack is not information. It is trust and love. They know Him, they hate Him, and they tremble.

So a man can hold every right doctrine and still be lost. That should not drive you to despair. It should drive you to Christ. Sound doctrine is the map, and you need it. But a map folded in the glovebox has never taken a man home. But do you want to know, vain man, that faith apart from works is dead? Vain means empty — a shell with nothing behind the words. The answer to emptiness is not more talk. It is a living Savior who fills. Christ did not come to add one more right answer to your head. He came to make a dead man live.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ABRAHAM ON THE MOUNTAIN
pulls: Abraham was declared righteous under the stars, with nothing in his hands. Decades later, on the mountain, his faith was shown to be exactly what God had already called it.
paras: Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar? Men use this verse to set James against Paul. Read it with your Bible open to Genesis. In Genesis 15:6, Abraham stood under the stars and believed the promise, and the Lord credited it to him for righteousness.
