That was the day he was declared right with God — by faith, with nothing in his hands. The mountain in Genesis 22 came decades later, after the son of promise had been born and grown.

So what does James mean by justified? He tells you in the next breath: You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected. On the mountain, Abraham’s faith was shown to be what God had already called it. God said so there: now I know that you fear God. The tree had been planted years before, with the root in the promise. The mountain was the day the fruit hung where anyone could see it. So the Scripture was fulfilled. The old verdict was proven true in the open, and Abraham was called the friend of God.

You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith. Not by a faith that only says. By a faith that does. Paul tells you what saves: faith alone, resting on Christ alone. James tells you what that faith looks like with the knife in its hand. And notice where the knife never fell. God provided the ram. Abraham had gone up the mountain concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead. Later, on a hill outside Jerusalem, the Father didn’t spare his own Son. He gave what He spared Abraham from giving, and He gave it for you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: A BODY WITH BREATH IN IT
paras: Then James sets a second witness beside the patriarch, and he could not have picked a sharper contrast. Wasn’t Rahab the prostitute also justified by works, in that she received the messengers and sent them out another way? Abraham was the father of a nation. Rahab was a Canaanite woman with a name in town, living in the wall of a city marked for judgment. She had heard what the Lord had done, and she believed: Yahweh your God, he is God in heaven above, and on earth beneath. Then she hid the men and let them down by a cord through her window. Her faith had a roof and a rope.

If James can stand Abraham and Rahab side by side, no man is too high to need grace and no man too low to be given it. Hebrews counts her among the faithful: By faith, Rahab the prostitute didn’t perish. Matthew writes her into the line of Christ, the mother of Boaz, in the family David came from.

For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead. You came from dust. Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Without the breath, the body is clay on a table. Faith without its works is like that: shaped right, lying still.

So where does the breath come from? Not from you. On the evening of the first day of the week, the risen Christ stood among frightened men behind a locked door. He breathed on them, and said, Receive the Holy Spirit. The life in your faith is His life. Your works are not the price of being saved. They are the breath of a man who already is.

stations.verse: And if a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food.
stations.question: When someone near me lacks what he needs for today, do I meet the need in front of me, or do I hand him a promise about later?
stations.live: Find one need this week that is measured in a day — a meal, a ride, a bill due Friday. Meet it before the day is out, and do not mention it to anyone.
body: Ephēmeros joins epi, upon, to hēmera, day. It means lasting for a day, or what is needed for the day. This is the only place it appears in the New Testament. James is not talking about a pantry stocked for winter. He is talking about tonight’s supper, and the table that is empty when it should not be.

That is what makes the brush-off so cold. The need is small and it is now. A man short of today’s bread does not need a talk about budgeting or a promise to circle back. He needs a sack of groceries before dark. Living faith answers on the clock the need is on.

The dust says somebody else will handle it, and later is good enough. But your Father has fed you every day of your life, before you thought to ask, and Christ taught you to ask again tomorrow. A man fed daily by grace can spare one day’s bread for his brother.

stations.verse: And one of you tells them, “Go in peace. Be warmed and filled;” yet you didn’t give them the things the body needs, what good is it?
stations.question: When I tell a struggling man I will pray for him, is that the end of my help or the start of it?
stations.live: Think of the last time you said ‘I’ll pray for you’ and left it there. Go back this week with the prayer and something in your hands: a coat, a check, a hot meal, an afternoon.
body: Thermainō comes from thermos, hot. It means to warm, and in the form James uses, to warm oneself. It appears five times in the New Testament. The other four all stand in one place: the high priest’s courtyard, at a fire of coals, where Peter stood warming himself.

Set the two scenes side by side. In James, a man tells the shivering to get warm and keeps his own coat. In the courtyard, Peter warms his own hands while his Lord is struck inside, and when they ask him, he says I am not. It is the same sin: comfort kept close while someone else stands in the cold.

The dust says a man who failed like that is finished. Peter was not. The Lord turned and looked at Peter, then went to the cross for him, rose, and called him back by name. Christ was stripped so you could be clothed. A man warmed by that grace can go and warm someone else.

stations.verse: You believe that God is one. You do well. The demons also believe, and shudder.
stations.question: Do I take comfort in knowing the right things about God, even where that knowledge has not moved me to trust Him?
stations.gloss: to shudder; to bristle with fear
stations.live: Write out three things you believe about God. Beside each, write one way it has moved your hands or your mouth this month. Where the second column is blank, ask Christ for life there.
body: Phrissō first meant to be rough, to bristle — the way the hair stands up on your arms. From there it came to mean to shiver or shudder with fear. It appears only here in the New Testament.

James uses it of the demons. They believe God is one. They are right about Him. And their right belief does not bring them near; it makes them shake. Knowledge without trust ends in dread. A man can know his catechism cold and still bristle at the thought of standing before God, because he has the facts and not the Friend.

The dust wants you to think fear is the most faith can feel. But you were not saved by facts about God held at arm’s length. You were saved by the Son of God, who took on Himself the wrath that makes demons tremble. In Him you can come near without bracing for the blow. The judgment that should make you shudder has already fallen on Christ.

stations.verse: But do you want to know, vain man, that faith apart from works is dead?
stations.question: Is my faith at work in my house and on my job, or is it standing idle in the market while the day runs out?
stations.live: Name one place your faith has been standing idle — the son you have not called, the help you keep meaning to give. Go to work there before Saturday: ‘I was hired late, and paid in full.’
body: Argos is built from a-, not, and ergon, work. It means idle, inactive, and of things, useless. Where your English Bible reads dead, many Greek copies read argos: a faith that does no work.

Jesus used the word of men in the marketplace late in the day. The owner of the vineyard asked them, Why do you stand here all day idle? They answered, Because no one has hired us. He sent them into the vineyard at the eleventh hour, and at sundown they were paid a full day’s wage. That is the shape of grace. Idle men were put to work and paid beyond their hours.

The dust says it is too late in the day for you to be of any use. But the Owner is still walking out to the market. Faith that stood idle can be hired yet. The vineyard is His, the wage is His, and the call to come is still open.

stations.verse: In the same way, wasn’t Rahab the prostitute also justified by works, in that she received the messengers and sent them out another way?
stations.question: Has my faith cost me anything at my own front door this year, or does it stay where it is safe?
stations.live: Open your door this week to someone who cannot pay you back — a widower, a new man at church, your son’s friend with no father at home. Set a plate for him at your table, and let him see your house as it is.
body: Hypodechomai joins hypo, under, to dechomai, to receive. It means to receive under your roof, to take someone in as a guest. Luke uses it of Martha taking Jesus into her house, and of Zacchaeus, who hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.

Rahab took the messengers in when taking them in could have cost her life. That was her faith, made visible in a door left open and a cord let down from a window. Faith that believes God is God in heaven above, and on earth beneath will sooner or later open the house. It will set another plate and give up the couch.

The dust says your house is too dirty for that kind of faith. Zacchaeus had more reason to think so than you do. But Jesus invited Himself in first: today I must stay at your house. He welcomed you before you ever welcomed anyone, and a welcomed man can open his door.

practices.title: SAY THE GOSPEL BEFORE THE LIST
practices.body: Before you write the day’s work on the back of an envelope, say what God has already done. By grace you have been saved through faith — not of works, that no one would boast. Then say the next line too: you are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them. The work comes second. It always comes second. Let the order of the words set the order of your morning, and the order of your week.

practices.title: MEET ONE DAY’S NEED
practices.body: Your Father has fed you every day of your life. Look this week for one need measured in a day — a meal for the family whose dad is laid up, a ride to the clinic, the light bill due Friday. Meet it before the sun goes down. Do not wait for a program to form or a committee to meet. James says the brother lacks daily food. Daily food is not a long-range problem. It is supper, and someone is hungry tonight.

practices.title: GO BACK WITH YOUR HANDS FULL
practices.body: Think of the man you told you would pray for. Pray for him, then go back. Take a coat, a check, a casserole your wife made, or two hours with a shovel. Peter warmed his hands while his Lord stood in the cold, and Christ still came for him. You have been warmed by a grace that went all the way to the cross. Carry some of that warmth to his door, and stay long enough to drink the coffee.

practices.title: CHECK THE SECOND COLUMN
practices.body: Write three things you believe about God in plain words. Beside each one, write how it has moved your mouth or your hands this month. Do not use this to grade yourself. You are already declared righteous in Christ, the way Abraham was under the stars. Use it to find the places where you need His breath. Where the second column is blank, pray over that line and ask Him for life there. He gives life to the dead.

practices.title: SET ONE MORE PLATE
practices.body: Rahab’s faith had a door and a rope. Yours can have a table and a few folding chairs. Invite one person this week who cannot return the favor — the widower down the road, the man new to your church, a young father with nobody to show him how. Jesus invited Himself into the house of a cheat and called it salvation. Welcome someone the way He welcomed you: first, on purpose, and before the house was clean.

title: Breath in the Body
subtitle: from dust to a living faith
keyVerse: For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.

passage.text: What good is it, my brothers, if a man says he has faith, but has no works? Can faith save him?
And if a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food,
and one of you tells them, “Go in peace. Be warmed and filled;” yet you didn’t give them the things the body needs, what good is it?
Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.
Yes, a man will say, “You have faith, and I have works.” Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works.
You believe that God is one. You do well. The demons also believe, and shudder.
But do you want to know, vain man, that faith apart from works is dead?
Wasn’t Abraham our father justified by works, in that he offered up Isaac his son on the altar?
You see that faith worked with his works, and by works faith was perfected.
So the Scripture was fulfilled which says, “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness,” and he was called the friend of God.
You see then that by works, a man is justified, and not only by faith.
In the same way, wasn’t Rahab the prostitute also justified by works, in that she received the messengers and sent them out another way?
For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.

stationsIntro: Read each verse aloud before you answer the question under it. Let the Greek word slow you down, and let it point you past your own hands to the hands of Christ.
lifeIntro: This week is not about proving to yourself that you are saved. It is about letting the life Christ gave you reach your hands, your wallet, and your front door.
lifePulls: Your works do not buy your place at God’s table. Christ bought it, all of it. Your works are what a fed man does when he sees a hungry brother at the door.
prayer: Father, You declared me righteous in Christ when I had nothing in my hands. Thank You that my standing with You rests on His cross and not on my week. Forgive me for the warm words I have spoken and left cold. Forgive me for knowing about You while I kept You at arm’s length. Breathe on the faith You gave me, and let it move my hands today. Give me eyes for the need that is measured in a day. Open my door the way You opened Yours to me. Let my hands this week show what You have already done in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You declared me righteous in Christ when I had nothing in my hands.
Thank You that my standing with You rests on His cross and not on my week.
Forgive me for the warm words I have spoken and left cold.
Forgive me for knowing about You while I kept You at arm’s length.
Breathe on the faith You gave me, and let it move my hands today.
Give me eyes for the need that is measured in a day.
Open my door the way You opened Yours to me.
Let my hands this week show what You have already done in me.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: James is not adding works to faith as a price. He is showing you what living faith does. Faith alone justifies: Abraham was counted righteous under the stars with empty hands. But the faith that justifies is never alone. It feeds the hungry brother, opens the door, and climbs the mountain. The dust says talk is enough, or that you must earn your place. Rest in Christ, and let His life reach your hands.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and leave the ledger where it lies. Leave the good deeds you count to feel safe and the cold ones you count to feel condemned. Leave the creed you have said for years with your arms folded. Lift your eyes to Jesus Christ, whose obedience never once stood idle, whose words were never empty, and whose whole perfect life is counted to you.

You were not saved by your hands. You were declared right with God the way Abraham was — under an open sky, believing a promise, holding nothing. The verdict did not wait for the mountain, and it does not wait for your next good week. Christ was delivered up for your sins and raised for your justification. The court has closed. Nothing you do this week will reopen it. Abraham came down the mountain with his son alive because God provided a ram in the thicket. You will come up out of the grave because God provided a Lamb and did not spare Him.

But He did not leave you a body lying on a table. On the evening of the first day of the week, the risen Christ came and stood in a locked room among men who had run from Him, and he breathed on them. That breath is in you now. It is why your hands can open, why your door can swing wide, why you can carry a sack of groceries down a cold drive and mean it. Your works are not your ticket in. They are the proof that Someone breathed.

So when the dust tells you your faith is dead, do not answer with a list of what you have done. Go to the God who breathed into the dust of the ground and made a living soul. Go to the valley of dry bones, where the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet. Go to the risen Lord in the locked room. He is still breathing on dust, and what He has made alive He will not leave lying still. The same breath that raised Him will raise your body on the last day, and stand you on your feet with your hands full of work He prepared for you.
closingVerse: For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.
carry: Where has your faith been speaking warm words with cold hands — and what would it look like this week to let the breath Christ gave you reach the need in front of you?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man has a sentence he would buy back if he could. The one you said to your son in the truck after he backed the trailer into the gatepost. The one about your wife that got a laugh on the job site. The text you sent at eleven at night after the second drink. You said it in four seconds. Some of it is still smoking in the people who heard it. You have apologized, or you have not. Either way, you know the words got out ahead of you and did their work before you could call them back.

The dust has two answers for that. The first is a shrug: it was just talk, that is how I am, they know I don’t mean it. The second is a clenched jaw and a vow — never again — and you will mean it right up until Thursday. One lie says your mouth is a small thing. The other says you can tame it with enough grit. Both leave the fire burning, and both leave you alone with it.

James says both are wrong. The tongue is small, and it is not harmless. And no man can tame it. That is not where hope ends. It is where hope starts, because a man who has run out of grit is ready to pray Psalm 119:25: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word of James 3 is that there is one Man who never stumbled in word, and His hand can take the bit.

sections.heading: A Letter That Keeps Coming Back to the Mouth
pulls: No man can tame the tongue. That is not the end of hope. It is the place hope starts, because the one Man who never stumbled in word can take the bit for you.
paras: James cannot leave the mouth alone. He has told you to be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. He has said a man’s religion is worthless if he doesn’t bridle his tongue (1:26). He will come back to it with slander (4:11) and with oaths (5:12). Here in 3:1–12 he gives the subject its fullest treatment and fills it with things a working man can picture: a bit, a rudder, a spark, a tamed animal, a spring, a fig tree.

He starts with teachers, because a teacher’s tools are words and he will answer for them. But he does not stay there. For we all stumble in many things. James is the Lord’s brother, counted among the pillars in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9), and he does not exempt himself. You are not reading a lecture from a man who has his mouth under control. You are reading a confession, written by a man who needed the same grace you do. John records that the Lord’s brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:5). The brother who once doubted now writes as a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace reached his mouth too.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE MAN WHO NEVER STUMBLED
paras: Let not many of you be teachers, my brothers, knowing that we will receive heavier judgment. James is not trying to empty the pulpit or the Sunday school room. He is telling men to count the weight before they pick it up. The teacher works with words, and words handed out in God’s name will be weighed by God. If you teach a class, lead your house in prayer, or open the Bible with your boys at the supper table, you are carrying something heavy. Carry it with fear, and with joy.

Then he levels the ground. For we all stumble in many things. Not some men — all of them. Not in one thing, but in many. Stumbling is not walking off a cliff on purpose. It is a man catching his boot on the same root, on the same path, in the same dark, again.

Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also. Read that with a straight face, and you will not find yourself in it. You will find one Man. Peter wrote of Him, neither was deceit found in his mouth, and When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. Jesus Christ is the perfect man James describes. His tongue never slipped. He bridled His whole body all the way up the hill to the cross, where He could have called for rescue and did not. And His obedience — every word He spoke and every word He held back — is counted to you by faith. You do not start this week trying to earn a clean mouth. You start it covered by His.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: SMALL THINGS THAT STEER
paras: Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body. An animal that outweighs you many times over goes where a few ounces of iron tell it to go. Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.

James is saying that the small thing steers the big thing. Your mouth is a few inches of muscle, and it turns your marriage, your crew, your boy’s picture of what a father sounds like, your name in town. So the tongue is also a little member, James says, and it brags of great things. It is small. It is never minor. A word at the breakfast table can set the course of a whole day in your house, and a word at a graveside can set the course of a life. Men carry what their fathers said to them long after the fathers are buried.

But notice who is holding the bit, and whose hand is on the rudder. The horse does not bridle itself. The ship does not steer itself through the wind. In James’s picture there is always a rider and always a pilot. Left alone, your tongue goes wherever the wind is blowing — the mood, the crowd, the grudge. Under Christ’s hand, the same small thing can turn a whole life toward home. That is why the first answer to your mouth is not a technique. It is a Master, and He has already bought you. A man does not hand his reins to a stranger. He hands them to the One who went to the cross for him and came back out of the grave.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ONE SPARK, A WHOLE HILLSIDE
pulls: The tongue is lit from below. No vow you make on the drive home will put it out. It takes a stronger fire, from above, and a Savior who took the curse.
paras: See how a small fire can spread to a large forest. You have seen it. A burn pile in March, a gust out of the west, and by dark the fire line is half a mile off and the volunteer fire department is lined up on the county road. And the tongue is a fire. One sentence and a marriage is smoking. One rumor and a church splits down the middle. One word at a family supper and two brothers do not speak for ten years.

Then James goes further than you want him to. The tongue defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna. The fire in your mouth is not your own invention. It is lit from below. That is why it spreads the way it does, and why it is so hard to put out. A sharp word is never just a mood.

Men have done hard things with animals. For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature, is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind. Oxen pull plows. Dogs work cattle. Falcons come back to the glove. But nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison. Read the word nobody slowly. Not you, not your pastor, not the man with thirty years of sobriety.

That sentence is meant to empty your hands. Your resolve will not put out a fire lit from below. It takes a fire from above. At Pentecost the Spirit came down in tongues like fire, and frightened men opened their mouths and spoke the mighty works of God. The same Spirit lives in you, and He has not come to make you quieter only. He has come to make your mouth His.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: ONE SPRING, ONE WATER
paras: With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God. Sunday morning you sing. Monday at seven you are calling the man who shorted the load a name you would not say in front of your mother. Same mouth. James says the man you cursed bears God’s image, the image you bear. To curse him is to spit on the likeness of the One you praised the day before. James does not let you split your life into Sunday and the rest.

Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so. Then James walks you outside. Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, yield olives, or a vine figs? What comes out tells you what is down in the ground. Jesus said it plainly: out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.

So the cure is at the source. You will not fix the water by painting the pipe. God has to change the spring — and in Christ, He has. Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth (1:18), and He planted that word in you. He also dealt with your cursing at the root. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. He hung on the tree under the curse your mouth deserved. The One who took the curse can teach a cursing mouth to bless. That is not a slogan. It is a cross, an empty tomb, and a living Lord who is not finished with you.

stations.verse: For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.
stations.question: When my words have done damage, do I try harder to rein in my mouth on my own, or do I put my whole body under the hand of Christ?
stations.gloss: to bridle; to lead by the bit
stations.live: Each morning this week, before your feet hit the floor, hand Him the reins out loud: ‘Lord Jesus, lead my mouth today. Where it pulls, pull it back.’
body: Chalinagōgeō joins chalinos, a bridle, to agō, to lead. It means to lead with a bridle, and so to rein in, to hold back. It appears twice in the New Testament, both times in James: once of the tongue (1:26), and here of the whole body.

Look at the order. The man who does not stumble in word is able to bridle the whole body also. The mouth is where the reins are held. A man who curses the stuck bolt will soon throw the wrench. A man whose mouth is reined can be led anywhere his Master wants him to go.

The dust says you are a wild thing and always will be. But a bridle means a rider. Christ has not left you to break yourself. He bought you, and He holds the reins with hands that were nailed for you. Being led by Him is not losing. It is being brought home, one step and one word at a time.

stations.verse: Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.
stations.question: Which way have my words been turning the people closest to me this year — toward Christ, or away from Him?
stations.live: Pick one conversation you have every day — supper, the drive to school, the crew before work. Decide before it starts which way you want it to turn, and say one sentence that turns it there.
body: Pēdalion comes from pēdos, the blade of an oar. It is a rudder, the steering oar of a ship. It appears twice in the New Testament: here, and in Acts 27, where the sailors on Paul’s ship cast off the anchors and loosed the rudder ropes to run for the beach.

That ship was wrecked, but every man aboard reached land, because God had promised it: they all escaped safely to the land. The rudder did not save them. The Lord did. Still, a small blade turned a big hull. Your words do the same in your house — the mood at supper, the way your daughter thinks a man talks to a woman, what your son thinks of the church. You are always steering something.

The dust says your words do not count for much. James says the ship goes wherever the pilot desires. The question is whose hand is on the helm. Put your mouth in Christ’s hand, and He will steer your house by it.

stations.verse: And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
stations.question: What fire have I started with my mouth that is still burning in someone I love while I wait for it to burn out on its own?
stations.live: Name the fire. Go to the person this week and say it without excuse: ‘What I said was wrong. I am sorry. Will you forgive me?’ Then stop talking and let him answer.
body: Phlogizō comes from phlox, a flame. It means to set on fire, to burn up. It appears in only one verse of the New Testament, and James uses it twice there: the tongue sets on fire, and is set on fire. The Greek Old Testament uses it of the lightning in the hail on Egypt (Exodus 9:24) and of the fire that goes before the Lord (Psalm 97:3).

So the tongue is both the match and the tinder. It sets the course of life burning, and it is itself lit from somewhere else. That is why a man with a quick temper cannot just turn it down like a burner on the stove. The flame has a source deeper than his mood.

The dust says the damage is done and nothing grows on burned ground. But Christ walked into the fire of judgment for you. The flame that should have taken you took Him. The fire your mouth set is not bigger than the cross that answers it.

stations.verse: And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
stations.question: Do I treat my sharp words as a bad habit to manage, or as a fire with a source that only Christ can deal with?
stations.live: When a cutting word rises this week, stop and ask where it is coming from before it leaves your mouth. Then pray one line instead of saying it: ‘Christ took the fire. I will not set one.’
body: Geenna comes from the Hebrew name for the Valley of Hinnom, west and south of Jerusalem. From the time of King Ahaz it was a place of fire-worship. Josiah defiled it, and it became the city’s dump. In time its name became the word for the place of final punishment.

The word appears twelve times in the New Testament. Eleven of them are on the lips of Jesus. James, the Lord’s brother, is the only other voice to use it. Jesus tied it to the mouth too: the man who calls his brother a fool will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna. James says the fire in a cursing mouth is lit from that same pit.

The dust says hell is a word for other men. But the Lord who spoke most about Gehenna is the One who bore its judgment for you on the cross. His blood can put out what your mouth has caught from below.

stations.verse: But nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
stations.question: Where is my mouth most restless — at home, on the job, or in my own head where no one else can hear?
stations.live: Pick one hour this week to keep your mouth shut on purpose — no complaint, no comment, no correction. Use it to listen, and rest on this: ‘He lays my foundation.’
body: Akatastatos is built from a-, not, and the verb kathistēmi, to set down, to settle. It means unsettled, unstable — a thing that will not stay put. James used it in 1:8 of the double-minded man, unstable in all his ways. Here he uses it of the tongue: a restless evil.

The Greek Old Testament uses it in Isaiah 54:11, of the afflicted one tossed with storms, and not comforted. That is the tongue at its worst: storm-tossed, never at rest, jumping from complaint to boast to the cut. A restless mouth usually belongs to a restless heart.

Listen to what God says next to that storm-tossed city: I will set your stones, and lay your foundations with sapphires. The dust says you will always be unsettled. God says He lays the foundation, and Christ is the stone that holds. A mouth that rests on Him can learn to be still, because it no longer has to defend itself.

practices.title: HAND HIM THE REINS
practices.body: Start each day by remembering whose obedience covers you. Christ never stumbled in word, and His clean record is counted to you. Then give Him the bit before your feet touch the floor: ‘Lord Jesus, lead my mouth today.’ Say it again on the drive to work, and again at the back door before you walk into your house. You are not taming yourself. You are being led, by a Master who has never once lost a horse He paid for.

practices.title: PUT OUT ONE FIRE
practices.body: Name one sentence you said that is still burning in somebody — your wife, your son, the man on your crew. Christ has already carried that sin to the cross, so you do not have to hide it or defend it. Go to the person this week. Say what you said, call it wrong, and ask to be forgiven. No ‘but.’ No explaining. Then be quiet and let him answer. Whatever he says, you have done what you could, and the rest is in the Lord’s hands.

practices.title: TRACE THE WATER TO THE SPRING
practices.body: At the end of each day, write down one thing that came out of your mouth that you would not want played back. Then ask what was down in the ground: fear, pride, a grudge, envy of the man who got the contract. Bring that to Christ by name. He has given you a new heart by His word. Ask Him to keep digging at the spring until the water runs clean. He finishes what He starts, and He is patient with slow ground.

practices.title: BLESS THE MAN YOU CURSED
practices.body: Think of the man you have cursed under your breath this month — the foreman, the neighbor, the driver who cut you off. He bears the image of God. Christ, When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back, and He prayed for the men who nailed Him. This week, pray for that man by name every day, and ask God to do him good — at work, at home, in his soul. Speak well of him once where others can hear, and mean it.

practices.title: STEER ONE SUPPER
practices.body: Your words are a rudder in your house. Pick one supper this week and decide ahead of time to steer it. Say one thing that builds up each person at the table — something true and specific, not flattery. Paul says to speak so that it may give grace to those who hear. God has spoken grace to you in His Son. Let your family taste a little of it at the table, and see who talks next, and how.

title: Bit, Rudder, and Spark
subtitle: from dust to a tongue under Christ’s hand
keyVerse: For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.

passage.text: Let not many of you be teachers, my brothers, knowing that we will receive heavier judgment.
For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.
Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body.
Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.
So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature, is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind;
but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water?
Can a fig tree, my brothers, yield olives, or a vine figs? Thus no spring yields both salt water and fresh water.

stationsIntro: Take these slowly, one a day if you can. This is a week about the mouth, so say each verse out loud before you answer the question, and let the Greek word open it.
lifeIntro: The hand that was nailed for your sins now holds the reins of your mouth. He bought the horse and the bit together. This week you learn what a led tongue sounds like.
lifePulls: The cure for a cursing mouth is not a tighter jaw. It is a new spring. God changes the water at the source, and He paid for the change with the blood of His Son.
prayer: Father, I have blessed You and cursed my brother with the same mouth. I cannot tame my tongue, and I am done pretending I can. Thank You that Jesus never stumbled in word, and that His obedience is counted to me. Thank You that He became a curse for me, so my cursing does not have the last word. Put out the fire in my mouth with the fire of Your Spirit. Change the spring, so that what comes out of me is fresh water. Take the reins today, at home and on the job. Let someone hear grace from me before this day is over. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have blessed You and cursed my brother with the same mouth.
I cannot tame my tongue, and I am done pretending I can.
Thank You that Jesus never stumbled in word, and that His obedience is counted to me.
Thank You that He became a curse for me, so my cursing does not have the last word.
Put out the fire in my mouth with the fire of Your Spirit.
Change the spring, so that what comes out of me is fresh water.
Take the reins today, at home and on the job.
Let someone hear grace from me before this day is over.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Your tongue is small, and it steers your whole life. It sets fires it cannot put out, and it is lit from below. No man can tame it — not you, not anyone. But one Man never stumbled in word, and He took your curse on the cross. Put your mouth in His hand. He changes the spring, holds the reins, and teaches a cursing mouth to bless. Start with the next sentence.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and let the words you cannot take back lie where they fell. Let the sentence in the truck lie there, and the comment on the job site, and the text you sent too late at night. Let the vow you made to do better and broke by Thursday lie there too. Lift your eyes to the only mouth that never stumbled — to Jesus Christ, a perfect person, the one James describes, who bridled His whole body all the way to the cross and never once said a word He had to take back. Lift them there, and keep them there.

Watch Him when the fire came at Him. When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. Before His accusers He was silent, as a sheep that before its shearers is silent. Nailed to the wood, with men hurling words at Him from the foot of the cross, He opened His mouth and said, Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing. That is the tongue James says no man can tame. It was never wild, and every word it spoke on that hill was spoken for you.

And the mouth that prayed for His enemies has not gone quiet. He rose from the dead, and he lives forever to make intercession for them. Right now, while your own mouth is still learning, His is speaking to the Father on your behalf. He does not stumble there either. He does not lose the thread or forget your name. Your worst sentence is not the last word said about you in heaven. The accuser’s case is not the last word either. His is, and He speaks it with blood on His hands. So bring Him your lips the way Isaiah did — undone, a man of unclean lips, standing in the smoke. A coal came from the altar, and a word came with it: your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven. The altar is the cross now. The fire that touches your mouth there does not burn you; it cleans you. Christ took the burning so the coal could come to you as mercy. And the Spirit who came down in tongues like fire will keep teaching your mouth to bless, until the day you stand before His face and open it in praise, with nothing left to take back.
closingVerse: For we all stumble in many things. Anyone who doesn’t stumble in word is a perfect person, able to bridle the whole body also.
carry: What sentence of yours is still burning in someone you love — and will you bring it this week to the One who never stumbled in word and who is speaking for you now?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust tells you wisdom is something a man earns with years. Enough winters behind him, enough scars on his hands, and he will know things. Some of that holds. A man who has poured forty slabs knows when the mix is too wet. A man who has buried his father knows which words to leave unsaid at a graveside. Years do teach.

But the dust has a second lie folded inside the first. It says wisdom is what you know and how well you say it. The man who wins the argument at the supply counter. The man whose opinion closes the meeting at church. The man who reads a room faster than anyone in it and lets everyone know he did. James walks into that room and does not ask what a man knows. He asks what grows out of him. A man can sit in a pew for a lifetime and still carry a bitter root and an elbow out for the best seat. A man saved last spring can already be gentle, easy to correct, quick to mercy. Age does not settle it. Fruit does.

That is a hard word for a man who has leaned on his own good sense. It means the wisdom you were proudest of may have been the dust talking all along. Psalm 119:25 is the cry of a man who has seen that about himself: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) And the reviving word of James 3 is that the wisdom you need does not rise up out of you. It comes down — and it has a face.

sections.heading: Two Wisdoms, Two Harvests
pulls: The dust says wisdom is what you know and how well you say it. James says wisdom is what grows out of you when no one is watching — and the wisdom from above came down in a Man before it ever came down in you.
paras: James has just spent twelve verses on the tongue — the bit, the rudder, the spark. Now he asks the question under it. Who is wise and understanding among you? The mouth is the spout. Wisdom is the spring. James, the Lord’s brother, is writing to scattered believers he calls the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion, churches where men were wrangling and reaching for the head of the room. He does not tell them to get smarter. He tells them there are two wisdoms, and each comes from a different place and grows a different crop.

One is from below. It is of the ground, of the flesh, and of the pit, and it grows confusion and every evil deed. The other is from above, and it grows peace. Read the six verses aloud before you go on. Notice that James never describes wisdom by what it knows. He describes it by how it lives. Then look hard at the list in verse 17. It reads like a portrait, because Someone lived it before you ever read it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: SHOWN IN THE WAY YOU LIVE
paras: Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom. James does not ask for credentials. He asks for a life. Wisdom in this letter is not a stock of answers. It is a way of carrying yourself — conduct, deeds, the daily handling of people and things. You show it in how you talk to the kid at the counter who got the order wrong, how you answer your wife when she is right, how you treat the man on the crew who will never be any use to you.

And the first mark James names is gentleness of wisdom. Not force. Not cleverness. Gentleness. That lands hard on a man who has made his way by being the strongest will in the room. But hear where it comes from. Jesus said, I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. The Son of God, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, carried His wisdom gently. He did not break the bruised reed. He knelt with a towel and washed feet that would run from Him before morning.

So before James asks anything of you, look at what has already come down. Christ was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption. You do not have to forge a gentle wisdom out of your own temper. It has been given to you in a Person, and He is not stingy with it. James told you so in his first chapter: God gives to all liberally and without reproach. Ask. Then let the gentleness show in your hands.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE BITTER SPRING
paras: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth. James goes under the ground now, down to the spring. A few verses back he asked whether one opening can send out fresh and bitter water. Here he tells you where the bitter comes from. Not the mouth. The heart — jealousy gone sour, ambition that has made itself the center of every job.

You know what it looks like. The man who got the promotion you trained him for, and you have not said his name kindly since. The brother at church whose work grew while yours stayed small. The quiet tally you keep of who gets thanked. James says do not dress that up as wisdom. Do not boast about your sharp read on people when the sharpness is resentment. That is lying against the truth with your whole posture.

Then he names it. This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic. Three steps down. Earthly — it never looks higher than the ground under your boots. Sensual — it runs on the appetites of the flesh. Demonic — it carries the family likeness of the one who took Jesus up a high mountain and offered Him the kingdoms of the world for one bow.

Hear the mercy in the naming. A doctor who tells you exactly where the rot is has not given up on the leg. James names the bitter spring because the Lord means to dig it out and give you a new one. Jesus stood up on the last day of the feast and cried, If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. The man with a bitter spring is the man He was calling.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: CONFUSION AND EVERY EVIL DEED
pulls: Jealousy promises to get you what you are owed. It hands you confusion and every evil deed instead. Christ walked into that wreckage as a servant, and He carried every grasping deed to the cross.
paras: For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed. Follow the bitter water downhill and see what it waters. Confusion first. A crew where every man is watching his own back stops building and starts jockeying. A house where the father must always win becomes a house where nobody tells him anything true. A church where men want the credit splits over the color of the carpet and calls it principle. Nobody in any of those places is short on opinions. They are short on peace.

Then every evil deed. James does not say some. Jealousy is a seed with a long reach. Cain watched God accept his brother’s offering and pass over his own. His face fell, and before long his hand rose against Abel in the field. Selfish ambition does not stay in its lane either. It starts as wanting the credit and ends as needing the other man to fail. Give it room and it will shade the numbers, cut the corner, run down a brother, and call all of it getting things done.

But do not stop at the wreckage. Look at who walked into it. On the night He was betrayed, Jesus sat at a table where a dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest. He did not out-argue them. He said, I am among you as one who serves. Then He went out and carried the evil deeds of jealous, grasping men to a cross. Every one of yours went with them. The confusion your ambition made in your house is not the last word spoken over it. The blood of the One who made peace is.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE WISDOM THAT COMES DOWN
paras: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. Read that slowly and ask whose life it describes. Pure — no hidden motive under the work. Peaceful — He came to make peace, not to win. Gentle — He would not quench a smoking wick. Reasonable — in the garden He bent His will to the Father’s. Full of mercy — He prayed for the men driving the nails. Without partiality — He ate with tax collectors and with Pharisees. Without hypocrisy — what He was in the light, He was in the dark.

This is not a ladder for you to climb. It is a portrait of Christ, and the wisdom from above is His life handed down into yours by His Spirit. It begins first pure, because a clean heart comes before a peaceful one, and He is the One who cleans it.

Then James ends with a farmer’s line. Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace. Peace is the harvest, and it is also the field the seed goes into. Jesus said unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. He went into the ground for you, and the tomb could not keep Him. From that grave came a harvest of righteousness, and you are part of it. So go plant peace this week where jealousy has been sowing. You scatter seed from a harvest already brought in, and the Lord of that harvest walks the rows with you.

stations.verse: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth.
stations.question: When someone else is honored for work I had a hand in, what comes up out of me first — gladness for him, or something sharp I keep to myself?
stations.gloss: sharp; bitter to the taste, then bitter in the heart
stations.live: Name the man you have not spoken of kindly since he passed you. Before Friday, say one true good thing about him to someone else, and pray for him by name: ‘Lord, bless him the way You have blessed me.’
body: Pikros first meant sharp or pointed, then sharp to the senses — bitter on the tongue. From there it moved inward to the man himself: harsh, bitter. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in this chapter.

The first is the spring in 3:11 that cannot send out fresh and bitter water from one opening. The second is 3:14, bitter jealousy. James has run a pipe from the water to the heart. The taste of your words comes from the spring under them. A man can sweeten his speech for an afternoon. He cannot sweeten the spring.

The dust says your bitterness is only honesty about how you were treated. Pikros says it is a taste, and everyone at your table can taste it. But Jesus offered living water to a woman with a whole well of reasons to be bitter. He has not stopped offering it, and He offers it to men exactly like you.

stations.verse: This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic.
stations.question: When I make a decision about money, my work, or my family, does my thinking ever look higher than the ground I am standing on?
stations.live: Take one decision in front of you this week — a purchase, a job offer, a hard talk with your son. Before you settle it, pray out loud: ‘Lord, show me what You want here, not just what pencils out.’
body: Epigeios is built from epi, upon, and gē, earth: of the earth, upon the ground. It occurs six times in the New Testament. Jesus uses it of earthly things. Paul uses it of the body as the earthly house of our tent.

The word is not an insult. You are made of dust, and the earth is the Lord’s. The trouble is a wisdom that never looks up from it. Paul describes men who think about earthly things and nothing more. That is what James names: a mind that plans the next quarter, the next truck, the next win, and never once asks what God wants.

The dust wants your horizon to stop at the fence line. But in the same conversation where He spoke of earthly things, Jesus named Himself as he who descended out of heaven. The wisdom from above put on an earthly tent and walked your ground. You do not have to climb up to it. He came down.

stations.verse: This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic.
stations.question: Where has my own cleverness looked less like the gentleness of Christ and more like the enemy who offered Him a shortcut to the throne?
stations.gloss: demon-like; having the look of a demon
stations.live: Find the shortcut you have been tempted to take — the shaded number, the convenient silence, the quiet word against a rival. Refuse it this week and say: ‘Jesus would not bow for a crown. I will not bow for this.’
body: Daimoniōdēs joins daimonion, a demon, to eidos, form or look. It means demon-like, having the look of a demon. This is the only place it appears in the New Testament.

James puts it last in his list. Earthly wisdom slides down to the sensual, then lower still. At the bottom it wears the family likeness of the one who showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world, and their glory and asked for a single bow. That is the devil’s wisdom: the crown without the cross. Jealousy and selfish ambition talk the same way. Take the shortcut. You have earned it.

The dust says your scheming is only being smart. Daimoniōdēs calls it by its family name. But Jesus refused the shortcut and took the long road through the cross to the throne. He would not bow. Because He would not, you are no longer owned by the one who asked Him to.

stations.verse: For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.
stations.question: What has my jealousy actually built in my home or my work that I would not want carried out into the daylight?
stations.live: Pick one thing jealousy has built — the cold shoulder, the hoarded credit, the cutting remark. Carry it into the light this week. Confess it to God, then to the man it touched. Christ has already carried it; you are only setting it down.
body: Phaulos first meant slight, worthless, of no account. In the New Testament it always carries a moral edge: worthless, bad. It occurs six times, and several times it is set against good.

The WEB renders it every evil deed. Keep the older sense close. What jealousy builds is cheap. It looks like getting ahead and comes to nothing worth keeping. Jesus said everyone who does evil hates the light, because cheap work does not want an inspector.

The dust wants you to keep the cheap work in the dark. But Paul says every believer will be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ, with deeds good or bad. Bring them into the light now, while the light is mercy. The Judge at that seat is the One who already bore your sins on the cross. His light does not come to shame you. It comes to make you clean, the way a man hoses mud off a son he loves.

stations.verse: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
stations.question: When my wife, an elder, or a brother on the crew tells me I am wrong, am I a man who can be persuaded, or a man who must always win?
stations.live: The next time someone corrects you this week, do not defend yourself for a full day. Pray over what they said. Then go back and tell them plainly what you found true in it.
body: Eupeithēs joins eu, well, to peithomai, the verb behind obeying. It means ready to obey, compliant — a man who yields. The WEB renders it reasonable. This is its only appearance in the New Testament.

Many men think a hard jaw is the mark of wisdom. James says the wisdom from above can be talked to. It hears correction without bristling. It yields to the truth when the truth comes from a younger man, or from your wife across the supper dishes. That is not weakness. It is a man who no longer needs to win.

The dust says giving ground is losing. But look at the garden. The Son fell on His face and prayed, not what I desire, but what you desire. He yielded, and His yielding saved you. You can afford to be persuaded. Your standing was settled by His obedience, not by your record of being right.

practices.title: ASK FOR IT FIRST
practices.body: James already told you God gives to all liberally and without reproach. Before the work starts each morning this week, ask Him plainly for wisdom in one named situation — the hire, the son, the money. Write it on a scrap of paper and keep it in your shirt pocket. At the end of the day, take it out and tell Him what you saw. He does not scold a man for asking, and He does not run short.

practices.title: TASTE THE WATER
practices.body: For three days, listen to how you talk about people who are not in the room — coworkers, neighbors, your pastor, your ex. Mark every sharp edge on a card. Do not argue with yourself about it. Just taste the water. Then bring the card to Christ and ask Him for the living water He offered a thirsty woman at a well. The spring is His to change, and He has already promised to change it.

practices.title: BLESS THE MAN WHO PASSED YOU
practices.body: Name the man whose success still sticks in your throat. Pray for his good by name every day this week. Then find one way to help him that he will never trace back to you. Bitter jealousy cannot keep its grip on a man who is quietly working for his rival’s good. Christ served the men who argued over the top seat at His own table. Because He served you, you can serve this one.

practices.title: BE PERSUADED ONCE
practices.body: Pick the person whose correction you resist the most. Ask them one direct question this week: ‘Where am I hard to talk to?’ Listen without a rebuttal. Write down what they said, even the part that stung. Thank them, and mean it. Christ bent His will to the Father in the garden, and your worth is settled by His obedience, not by your record of being right. You can afford to hear it, and to change.

practices.title: SOW ONE PEACE
practices.body: Find one place where your ambition has made confusion — a feud at work, a cold dinner table, a split in the men’s group. Do not wait for the other man. Go first. Make one concrete move toward peace this week: a phone call, a lunch, an apology with no excuses stapled to it. The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace. You are not raising the crop. The harvest is already the Lord’s.

title: Wisdom from Above
subtitle: from dust to the wisdom that comes down
keyVerse: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.

passage.text: Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.
But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth.
This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic.
For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

stationsIntro: Take each verse slowly and let it read you before you read it. Where a Greek word is opened, let it show you the root under the fruit, and then point you to the wisdom that came down to replace it.
lifeIntro: The wisdom from above has already come down in Christ, and God gives it to every man who asks, without reproach. This week, trace the bitter water back to its spring and ask for His in its place. Grit will not grow this crop; the One who gives it will.
lifePulls: You do not grow the wisdom from above by straining. It came down in Christ, it is given to the man who asks, and it shows up in gentle hands long before it shows up in clever words.
prayer: Father, You give wisdom to all liberally and without reproach, and I am asking. I confess the bitter jealousy I have called good sense. I confess the ambition that wanted the credit more than it wanted You. Thank You that Christ was made wisdom for me, and that His gentleness is mine in Him. Dig out the bitter spring in me and give me living water. Make me pure, peaceful, gentle, and easy to correct. Teach me to sow peace in my house this week. Let the harvest Christ planted by His death and resurrection show up in my hands. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You give wisdom to all liberally and without reproach, and I am asking.
I confess the bitter jealousy I have called good sense.
I confess the ambition that wanted the credit more than it wanted You.
Thank You that Christ was made wisdom for me, and that His gentleness is mine in Him.
Dig out the bitter spring in me and give me living water.
Make me pure, peaceful, gentle, and easy to correct.
Teach me to sow peace in my house this week.
Let the harvest Christ planted by His death and resurrection show up in my hands.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: James does not ask what you know. He asks what grows out of you. Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition pass themselves off as good sense, but they come from below and grow confusion and every evil deed. The wisdom from above came down in Christ — pure, peaceful, gentle, full of mercy — and God gives it without reproach to any man who asks. Taste your own water, ask for His, and go sow peace.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, because the wisdom you need is coming down. It will not come up out of the tally you keep of who got ahead of you. It will not come up out of the argument you won last week and the brother you lost in the winning. It will not come up out of the bitter spring you have drunk from for years and called experience. It comes down, and in Christ it has already come.

The dust told you a man is as wise as he is sharp. But James set a portrait in front of you, and it has a face. Pure and peaceful, gentle and reasonable, full of mercy, without partiality and without hypocrisy. That is Jesus Christ, who came down from heaven into an earthly tent, who took the towel at a table full of men arguing over who was greatest, who bent His will to the Father’s in the garden and prayed for the men who nailed Him to the wood. He did not only teach the wisdom from above. He lived every line of it in your place, and the Father counts His life as yours.

So look at the seed. He said a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die before it bears fruit. He went into the ground for you. He came up out of it as the first fruits of those who are asleep, and the harvest of righteousness began. You are part of that harvest. The Spirit He gave you is not a foreman grading your temper. He is a new spring in you, and He does not run dry. He was given to you on purpose, and He is not leaving.

Ask, then, and keep asking. God gives to all liberally and without reproach — He will not throw your past in your face when you come to Him for wisdom this week. Take the gentleness He gives and carry it into the kitchen, into the shop, into the meeting where you would rather win. Sow peace where you once sowed rivalry. Let the man who passed you see a brother where he expected a rival. The field is His, the seed is His, and the One who went into the ground for you is coming back for His harvest.
closingVerse: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
carry: Where have you been calling your bitterness good judgment — and what would change this week if you asked the God who gives without reproach for the wisdom that came down in Christ?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust tells you that what you want is what you need. A bigger shop, a wife who agrees with you more, a son who calls. The respect of the men who passed you over, and a few quiet hours with the phone and nobody asking anything of you. You want it, you do not have it, and the wanting sits in your chest like a coal that will not go out. And when you finally get it, it is never enough. The new truck smells new for about a month.

Then the dust tells you a second lie: that the fight in your house and the cold war at work are about the other man. If he would get out of the way. If she would just see it. James strips that down to the studs. Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Not from them. From you — from pleasures that war inside your own members. That is the first mercy in this chapter. A man who knows where the war starts can stop blaming the weather.

Then comes the third lie, and it is the heaviest. When you finally see it — the grasping, the side comments, the prayers that were really orders — the dust says you have used up God. You have gone to the well too many times with the same sin in the same bucket. He is done with you. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a man pinned under that weight: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) And the reviving word of James 4 is four words long: he gives more grace.

sections.heading: Hard Words to a Wandering Bride
pulls: The dust says you have used up God. James answers with four words that have outlasted every proud man who ever lived: he gives more grace. Not grace that keeps pace with your sin. Grace that outruns it.
paras: James has just painted the wisdom from above — pure, peaceful, gentle. Now he turns the lamp on the churches he is writing to, the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion, and the light is not flattering. Quarrels and grasping. Prayers bent toward appetite, and friendship with the world. He calls them adulterers. That is covenant language. Israel’s prophets used it of a people married to the Lord who went running after other lovers.

Do not hurry past the hard words to reach the soft one. Grace means little to a man who thinks he only needs a little help. Read these six verses aloud, slowly. Feel the weight of verses 1 through 5 settle on you. Then watch James do what God always does. He tells you the whole truth about yourself, and then He outgives it. Verse 6 is the title of this whole book, and it lands hardest on the man who has felt the first five verses.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE WAR INSIDE
paras: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members? James does not start with the devil or the culture. He starts under your own skin. The word behind pleasures is plain: the things a man is glad to have. Comfort. Respect. Money. Being left alone. None of them sit still. They war. They throw their weight around in your members — your hands, your eyes, your tongue, your wallet. A pleasure that rules a man is never content with what he has. It always wants the next thing, and it wants it now.

Then he lays out the chain. You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. Most men read murder and relax. But Jesus said the man who is angry with his brother stands in danger of the same judgment. The three days of silence toward your wife. The man you cut out of your life because he got what you wanted. The words in the parking lot after the ball game. It is the same war with the volume turned down. And the man who wins it still goes to bed hungry.

Then comes the line that turns the whole passage. You don’t have, because you don’t ask. You have been fighting men for things you could have asked your Father for. You have been grabbing with fists what He would have set in open hands. Jesus told you plainly: how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him. The war inside you is a hungry man fighting over crumbs under a table where his Father is already serving the meal. Stop fighting for the plate. Ask.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: ASKING TO SPEND
paras: You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures. Some men are already saying, I do ask. James knows. He says the asking itself can be bent. A man can pray for a raise so he can stop needing God. He can pray for his wife to change so he does not have to. He can pray for the business to grow when what he wants is to be the man everyone in the county knows. That is not prayer. That is placing an order.

The word spend is the same word Jesus used for the younger son, who spent all of it in a far country. That is the picture James sets in front of you: a son who takes his father’s good gifts and burns them on himself. A father who loves that son does not keep sending fuel for the fire.

But stay with the prodigal, because Jesus did not end the story in the pig yard. When the son came home broke and starving with a speech about being a hired hand, the father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. Then came the robe, the ring, the sandals. A son who had spent everything was given more than he ever spent.

So the answer to bent prayer is to come home and ask as a son. Ask for what the Father loves to give — a clean heart, wisdom, a love for your wife that keeps no score. And you do not pray alone. Christ lives forever to make intercession for those who come to God through Him. Your bent prayers are carried to the Father by a Priest whose prayers are never bent.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: A JEALOUS HUSBAND
pulls: God’s jealousy is not a small man’s insecurity. It is the right of a Husband who paid for His bride in blood. The Spirit who lives in you will not share you with a rival, because He wants all of you.
paras: You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? James reaches for the hardest word in a marriage. The prophets used it of Israel. The Lord took a people to Himself as a man takes a wife, and she ran after other lovers. Hosea was told to go love an adulteress, even as Yahweh loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods. James says that is what friendship with the world is. Not owning a television. Not working a job outside the church. It is handing your heart’s allegiance — your time, your money, your hope, your fear — to the order of things that has no room for God.

And you cannot keep both. Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God. A man cannot keep a woman on the side and call it a marriage. Neither can a soul. James is not asking whether you still go to church. He is asking who has your heart when the money runs short and the phone lights up at midnight.

Then verse 5, and the Husband’s heart shows. The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously. God’s jealousy is the right of a husband who paid for his bride. Hosea bought back the woman he was told to love, for silver and barley. Christ bought you back with His blood. The Spirit He sent lives in you, and He will not share you with a rival. Hear that as love. A husband who does not care whether his wife wanders does not love her. The Spirit’s jealousy over you is proof that you are wanted — wanted whole, wanted back, wanted for good.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: BUT HE GIVES MORE GRACE
paras: Everything in this passage has been running downhill. War inside, bent prayers, adultery, a jealous God. If James had stopped at verse 5, you would have every reason to stay face-down in the dirt. He does not stop. But he gives more grace.

Feel the size of that sentence. Your pride is large. Your grasping runs deep. Your friendship with the world has years on it. And God’s answer is not a shrug, and it is not a ceiling. It is more. Paul says it from the other side of the same hill: where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly. Grace does more than keep pace with your sin. It outruns it. You have not gone to the well too many times. The well is Christ, and He does not run dry.

Then James quotes Proverbs. God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Watch the order. God gives first. Humility does not earn the grace or pound it loose from a locked door. Humility is only the shape of a man with open hands. The proud man’s hands are full — his record, his rights, his reasons — and God stands against him the way a guardrail stands against a truck headed for the ditch. The humble man has nothing in his hands but need, and grace falls into them.

And where did that grace come from? From the cross. Christ humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. The sentence that belonged to the proud fell on the humble Son, so that proud men brought low could receive the Son’s reward. Every time you come empty-handed, you stand on ground He cleared for you. He gives more grace. Today. Again tomorrow. Again on the morning you are sure He is finished with you.

stations.verse: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
stations.question: What pleasure — comfort, respect, money, being left alone — am I most ready to fight the people closest to me to keep?
stations.gloss: pleasure; what a man is glad to have
stations.live: Name the pleasure you fought for this past month and the person you fought. Go to that person this week and say it without a single excuse: ‘I wanted my way more than I wanted you. I am sorry.’
body: Hēdonē comes from a verb meaning to be glad. It is simply pleasure. It appears five times in the New Testament, twice in these verses. James uses the plural — pleasures, many of them, each with its own claim on you.

Jesus used it in the parable of the sower. The seed among thorns is choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life. Pleasure is not the enemy. God made the meal, the rest, the marriage bed. But a pleasure that must be had becomes a soldier, and soldiers fight. James says these war in your members, and your family takes the fire.

Paul once described believers as serving various lusts and pleasures. Then came the turn: when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared. The dust says your pleasures are rights to defend. The kindness of God in Christ says they were masters, and you have been bought out from under them.

stations.verse: You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
stations.question: If God answered every prayer I prayed this month exactly as I asked it, who would end up richer — His kingdom and my family, or only me?
stations.gloss: to spend; to use up, squander
stations.live: Write down three things you have asked God for lately. Beside each, write the plain reason why. Then add one request you know the Father loves to give, and pray that one every morning this week.
body: Dapanaō means to spend, to pay out — and in a second sense, to use up, to squander. It occurs five times in the New Testament. A sick woman had spent all that she had on physicians. The younger son had spent all of it in a far country. James 4:3 belongs with the second.
The picture is a man who asks God for gifts so he can burn them on himself. The prayer is real. The motive is bent. God loves you too much to bankroll your far country.

But look at what became of both spenders. The woman who had spent everything came up behind Jesus in the crowd, touched His clothes, and was healed — and He called her Daughter. The son who had spent everything came home to a robe and a ring. The dust says you have spent too much to come back. Jesus keeps taking in people who are spent.

stations.verse: You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
stations.question: Where has my heart been keeping company with the world — giving it my fear, my hope, my best hours — while I still call myself the Lord’s?
stations.live: Name one place where the world has your heart — the screen, the market, the approval of certain men. Cut its hours in half this week, and give those hours back to your Lord and to your wife.
body: Moichalis means an adulteress, or used as an adjective, adulterous. It appears six times in the New Testament. Jesus used it of an evil and adulterous generation that demanded a sign from Him. The word is feminine, and it pictures a wife who has wandered.

That is how the Scriptures speak of God’s people. The Lord is the husband. His people are the bride. James is not singling out a few men who have cheated on their wives. He is telling every man in the church that a heart handed to the world is a bride unfaithful to the Husband who keeps her.

The dust says that kind of betrayal ends the marriage. But Paul says believers have been joined to him who was raised from the dead. Christ did not put away His wandering bride. He gave Himself up for her. The same word that convicts you tells you whose you are.

stations.verse: Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?
stations.question: Do I hear God’s jealousy over me as a threat to my freedom, or as proof that the Spirit living in me wants all of me and wants it for good?
stations.live: When you feel the Spirit’s pull away from a rival this week — a habit, a grudge, a screen — do not argue with it. Answer it out loud: ‘You want all of me. You may have it.’
body: Phthonos means envy. It occurs nine times in the New Testament, and everywhere else it names a sin — in Paul’s lists beside murder and strife, and in men who preach Christ even out of envy. In James 4:5 it stands behind the word jealously.

Its darkest use is in the Gospels. Pilate knew that because of envy they had delivered him up. Envy put Jesus on the cross. The very grasping James exposes in 4:1–2 is what handed the Son of God over to die.

Now see what God does with it. The sin that crucified Christ became the hour of your redemption, and the Spirit He poured out now longs over you with a holy jealousy. Man’s envy grabs to take. The Spirit’s jealousy holds on to keep. The dust says God’s jealousy is a fist. James says it is the yearning of the Spirit who lives in you and will not let you go.

stations.verse: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.
stations.question: Where am I still holding my hands full of my own record, rights, and reasons — too proud to come to God with nothing in them?
stations.live: Name one place where pride has kept your hands full — the help you refused, the sin you have not confessed. Empty it this week before God and one brother: ‘I have nothing here. I need more grace.’
body: Hyperēphanos joins hyper, above, to a verb meaning to show oneself: a man who shows himself above others. Outside Scripture it could even mean splendid. In Scripture it is always arrogant, haughty. It occurs five times in the New Testament, and twice it stands against the humble in the proverb James and Peter both quote.
