Pride is not only the loud man. It is the man who will not ask for help, will not confess, will not receive. Mary sang that God has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. He resists that man the way a father bars the gate against a son bent on ruin — for his good, and before the fall.

The dust says humility is the price you pay for grace. James says God gives first, and the humble man is simply the one with empty hands. Christ humbled himself all the way to the cross so that proud men could be emptied and filled. Come with nothing. He gives more.

practices.title: TRACE ONE FIGHT HOME
practices.body: Take the last real fight you had — with your wife, your son, a man at work. Sit down at the table with a pencil and trace it back. What pleasure was at stake? Comfort, respect, money, being left alone? Name it plainly. James says the war started in your members, not in theirs. Then go back to that person and own your half without a single ‘but’ attached. Christ has already covered it; you are free to say it.

practices.title: ASK INSTEAD OF GRAB
practices.body: You don’t have, because you don’t ask. Find one thing you have been trying to take by force — control at work, agreement at home, a quick fix for an old problem. This week, stop working the angles for it. Bring it to the Father in plain words every morning. Your Father knows what you need before you ask Him. Leave it in His hands and watch what He does with it. A son asks. Only an orphan grabs, and you are no orphan.

practices.title: STRAIGHTEN YOUR PRAYERS
practices.body: Write down what you have prayed for this past month. Beside each, write the plain reason. Some will be good. Some will be fuel for your own pleasures. Do not tear the list up in shame. Take it to Christ, who lives forever to make intercession, and ask Him to straighten your asking. He was praying for you long before you started praying. Then pray every day for one thing the Father loves to give, and expect Him to give it.

practices.title: BREAK ONE FRIENDSHIP
practices.body: Name the friendship with the world that has your heart — the market, the screen, the approval of men whose respect you crave. Cut it down hard this week: an hour back every evening, a subscription cancelled, a habit broken. Give those hours to your wife, your children, and the Word. The Spirit who lives in you is jealous for them. He bought them with blood. Let Him have them, and see what He does with a man’s evenings.

practices.title: COME EMPTY-HANDED
practices.body: Each night this week, before you sleep, set your open hands on the table or the bed. Name one way you were proud that day. Then say out loud: But he gives more grace. Do not promise God you will do better tomorrow. Receive what Christ already bought for you. A humble man is only a man with nothing in his hands and grace falling into them. Go to sleep with your hands open.

title: More Grace
subtitle: from dust to grace that outruns your pride
keyVerse: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

passage.text: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.
You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?
But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

stationsIntro: These six verses wound before they heal. Let each word lay bare the want underneath the fight, and then let it carry you to a grace that is larger than the want.
lifeIntro: God gives more grace than your pride can use up, and He gives it first. So this week, trace your fights back to the want underneath them, bring your bent prayers home to the Father, and open empty hands.
lifePulls: Humility does not buy grace. Grace is already falling. Humility is only a man finally opening his hands — and Christ, who humbled Himself to the cross, has made sure there is always more to fall into them.
prayer: Father, I have fought men for what I should have asked You for. I have asked You for good things only to spend them on myself. I have given my heart to the world and still called myself Yours. Thank You that Your Spirit lives in me and yearns over me with a holy jealousy. Thank You that Christ humbled Himself to the cross for a proud man like me. Empty my hands of my record, my rights, and my reasons. Where I have grabbed, teach me to ask as a son. You resist the proud; bring me low enough to receive. You give more grace — give it to me again today. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have fought men for what I should have asked You for.
I have asked You for good things only to spend them on myself.
I have given my heart to the world and still called myself Yours.
Thank You that Your Spirit lives in me and yearns over me with a holy jealousy.
Thank You that Christ humbled Himself to the cross for a proud man like me.
Empty my hands of my record, my rights, and my reasons.
Where I have grabbed, teach me to ask as a son.
You resist the proud; bring me low enough to receive.
You give more grace — give it to me again today.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Your fights start inside you, in pleasures that want what you do not have. You grab instead of asking, and when you ask, you ask to spend it on yourself. You keep company with the world while the Spirit in you yearns jealously over you. And God still says: more grace. He gives first. Humility only opens the hands. Christ humbled Himself to the cross so a proud man could receive. Empty your hands.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the fight you have been winning at the cost of your house. Lift them off the thing you want and do not have. Lift them off the prayers you sent up like orders and the gifts you spent like a son in a far country. Lift them off the count you keep of how many times you have come back to God with the same sin in the same bucket. You have not used Him up. You never will.

The dust told you there was a limit and you were close to it. But James set four words in the middle of the hardest passage in his letter, and they hold like iron: he gives more grace. He did not say enough grace. He said more. More than your pride. More than your grasping. More than the years you spent keeping company with the world. Where your sin went deep, grace went deeper. Where your sin piled high, grace climbed over it. The well has no bottom, because the well is Christ.

Look at what it cost Him. The Son, existing in the form of God, emptied Himself and took the form of a servant. He let envious men hand Him over to Pilate. He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. He stood where the proud man stands — where you stood — and the judgment due the proud fell on Him, so that you could stand where the humble stand and be given grace. Then the Father raised Him from the dead and gave to him the name which is above every name. He lives now to intercede for you, and the Spirit He sent lives in you and yearns over you, and will not let a rival have you.

So come empty this week, and come again tomorrow. Come with the fight you started and the prayer you bent. Come with nothing in your hands but need. God does not wait for you to earn the gift or pound it loose. He gives first. The proud He resists; the humble He fills. Open your hands at the kitchen table on Tuesday morning, with the coffee going cold and the same old sin still in your mouth, and hear it again from the God who cannot lie: he gives more grace. Then stand up and go home a son.
closingVerse: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.
carry: What are you still holding in your hands — a grudge, a right, a record, a rival — that keeps you from receiving the more grace God is already giving you in Christ?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: A man learns early to keep his feet. You learned it on the ball field, in the shop, at the first job where the foreman watched to see who flinched. Stay up. Don’t let them see you on the ground. Your father may have said it in so many words. That is fair advice for a scuffle in a parking lot. It is ruinous advice for a sinner standing before a holy God.

The dust tells you that going low is the end of you. Admit the sin plainly and you lose the argument. Grieve it and you lose your nerve. Let God see you on your knees and He will leave you there, a little smaller each time. So you keep your feet. You manage the sin instead of mourning it. You laugh off what ought to break you. And you stay busy measuring the man in the next pew, because a man with a tape on his brother never has to kneel.

Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a man who has quit pretending he is standing: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) He does not ask to be spared the ground. He is already on it, face down. He asks to be raised, and he asks for it by the word.
James 4:7–12 is the word that raises him. Down is not where God leaves a man. Down is where God lifts him from. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

sections.heading: Ten Commands on One Floor
pulls: The dust says a man who goes down before God stays down. James says the ground is where God does His lifting — and the promise of 4:10 has no clause that leaves a humbled man lying in the dirt.
paras: Read these six verses aloud and count the commands. There are ten in the first four, coming like hammer strokes: be subject, resist, draw near, cleanse, purify, lament, mourn, weep, let your laughter be turned, humble yourselves. Then two more verses take the hammer to your tongue. A tired man reads a list like that at 5:40 in the morning and closes the book.

But look at the hinge. Be subject therefore to God. That word therefore points back one verse, to the sentence this whole letter rests on: But he gives more grace. Every command here stands on that floor. James is not handing you ten rungs to climb up to God. He is telling a man who has already been given grace what that grace does when it reaches the low places in him. God gives first. The bowed head receives. You do not have to pound on heaven’s door to get Him to open a hand that is already open. And the same grace that brings you down before God will shut your mouth about your brother, because a man on his knees has no room left to look down on anyone.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: SUBJECT, THEN STANDING
paras: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Watch the order. Submission comes before resistance, and the order matters. A man who has not bowed to God has no ground to stand on against the devil. He is only one rebel quarreling with another. To be subject is to line up under the One in command. You do not fight this war on your own terms. A hired man who will not take orders from the owner ends up quarreling with every hand on the place.

Then stand. James does not tell you to chase the devil, study him, or bargain with him. He tells you to resist — to plant your feet and refuse him the ground. The temptation that comes at 10:40 at night with the house quiet and the phone lit. The old bitterness that rises every time a certain name comes up. The pull toward the second drink after a long week. Each of them arrives sounding like your own voice, tired and owed something. To resist is to stop agreeing with it. You do not have to win the debate. You have to refuse the ground.

Can a man of dust do that? Not alone. But you do not stand alone, and you do not stand first. Jesus was led into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil, hungry and by Himself, and He did not fall where Adam fell. He answered each lie with the written word: Get behind me, Satan. Then He went to the cross, and by His death He brought to nothing the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil. You resist an enemy already beaten. That is why the promise is so plain. He will flee from you. Not might. Will.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: NEAR, AND WASHED
paras: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. The dust hears that as a bargain: you take the first step, and if the step is good enough, God takes the second. But James has just told you who moved first. He gives more grace. The father in Jesus’ story saw his son while he was still far off, and ran. Your drawing near is the answer to a God who came all the way down in His Son, and who now lives forever to make intercession for every man who comes to God through Him. The door you walk toward was opened from the other side, and it was opened with nails.

Then James gets specific. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded. Hands are what you did. Hearts are what you wanted. He names both because a man can scrub one and leave the other filthy. You can keep your hands off the thing and still nurse it in your heart for a year. You can feel sorry in your heart and leave your hands right where they were. James wants both washed — the deed and the desire, the outside and the in.

And he calls you by name: sinners, double-minded. He does not say it to shame you. He says it because no man gets washed who denies he is dirty. Here is the good news inside the hard word. The washing you need has already been provided. The blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin. You do not wash your way to God. You come to God and He washes you, and then your hands go to work like hands that have been made clean.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: LAUGHTER TURNED TO MOURNING
pulls: You were never hired to judge your brother. One Lawgiver holds that seat, and He shed His own blood for the man you were about to talk down.
paras: Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to gloom. This is not James scowling at every joke at the supper table. He is aiming at one kind of laugh — the one a man uses to keep his sin at arm’s length. The crack about how much you drink. The grin when someone mentions your temper. The shrug that says every man does it. That laughter is a fence around a sin, and James wants the fence torn down. As long as you can laugh at it, you never have to look at it.

Godly grief is not a mood you work up. It is what happens when a man finally sees his sin the way God sees it and stops defending it. Paul says godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. The dust has its own sorrow, the kind that only hates getting caught, and Paul says that kind produces death. James is not calling you into that pit. Grief over sin is not the enemy of joy. It is the road to the only joy that lasts. He is calling you to the place where Jesus said, Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.

Then comes the promise this whole week leans on. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you. You go down. He lifts. Nobody has walked that road farther than Christ. He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, all the way into another man’s tomb. Therefore God also highly exalted him. The tax collector who could not lift his eyes went down to his house justified. The ground before God is not the end of a man. It is where the lifting starts.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: ONE LAWGIVER, ONE JUDGE
paras: Then James turns from your knees to your mouth. Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He has the church in view — men who sit in the same pews and sing the same hymns. The side comment in the truck after the meeting. The sigh when a certain man stands up to pray. The story you tell at supper where you come out wise and your brother comes out a fool. You can do it without ever raising your voice. It feels like talk. James calls it something heavier.

He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. The law already told you what to do with your brother: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. When you talk him down, you are not only breaking that law. You are climbing onto a bench above it and ruling that it does not apply to this man, not today. You have quit being a doer of the law and made yourself its judge.

Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another? That question is not a sneer. It is relief. The seat is taken. The Father judges no one, but he has given all judgment to the Son, and the Son shed His blood for the brother you were about to cut down — and for you. The Judge of all the earth is the one Man with every right to speak against you, and instead He is at God’s right hand, who also makes intercession for us. A man who knows that can put the knife back in the drawer. He has been spared by the Judge. He has no stomach left for sentencing anyone else.

stations.verse: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
stations.question: When the old temptation comes back this week, what ground am I still handing it because I would rather bargain than stand?
stations.live: Name the hour the old temptation usually comes for you. When it comes this week, stand up, leave the room or set the phone down, and say aloud: ‘I am under God. You don’t get this ground.’
body: Anthistēmi joins anti, against, to histēmi, to stand. It means to withstand, to resist, to oppose — to set your feet and refuse to give ground. A dozen New Testament verses carry it, and Peter uses it of the same enemy James names: Withstand him steadfast in your faith.

Notice what the word does not mean. It does not mean attack, chase, or outwit. Paul uses it of a man in God’s armor who is able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Your task is not to win the war. Christ won it. Your task is to hold the ground He took and not hand it back.
The dust says the devil is too strong and you are too tired. Anthistēmi answers that the devil is beaten and you are not alone. Stand under God, and the promise is not a maybe: he will flee from you.

stations.verse: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
stations.question: What am I trying to scrub off by myself before I will come near to the God who makes unclean men clean?
stations.live: Name one thing your hands did this week that they should not have done. Bring it to God by name, then make it right with the man or woman it touched: ‘I came to be washed, not to prove I was clean.’
body: Katharizō means to cleanse, to make clean. Thirty New Testament verses carry it. The Gospels use it again and again of lepers. It reaches the inner man too: Peter says God was cleansing their hearts by faith, and John writes that the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin.

Look at the leper in Mark 1. He could not clean himself. He knelt and said Jesus could do it if He wanted to. Jesus stretched out his hand, and touched him, and said, I want to. Be made clean. The word James uses for your hands is the word Jesus spoke over that man’s skin.

The dust wants you to wash first and come later, after you have scrubbed off this week. Katharizō turns that around. Come to the One who makes clean, and then put your hands to work like hands that have been washed.

stations.verse: Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to gloom.
stations.question: Is there a sin I keep laughing off that I have never once let myself grieve in front of God?
stations.live: Take the sin you joke about. One evening this week, sit with it at the kitchen table without the joke. Name it to God plainly, read Luke 18:13–14, and say: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’
body: Katēpheia means dejection. It comes from an adjective meaning downcast — the look of a man whose head has dropped. This is the only place it appears in the New Testament, and James sets it at the end of his line: your joy to gloom.

Jesus told of a tax collector who wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven. He stood far off, compared himself to no one, beat his breast, and asked for mercy. That is the downcast look James means — not a man pitying himself, but a man who has stopped pretending before God. And Jesus said that man went home justified.

The dust offers two ways out: laugh it off, or sink and stay sunk. Katēpheia is neither. It sits one verse before he will exalt you. It is a doorway, not a place to live. God does not want you face down forever. He wants you face down long enough to be lifted.

stations.verse: Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law, but a judge.
stations.question: Which brother do I talk down when he is not in the room, while I call it concern?
stations.live: Choose the one man you most often talk down. For seven days say nothing against him to anyone. Pray for him by name each morning, and say one true, good thing about him where others can hear it.
body: Katalaleō joins kata, against, to laleō, to speak. It means to speak evil of, to rail at, to talk a man down. Outside James 4:11 the New Testament uses it only in 1 Peter, both times of what unbelievers say about Christians: they speak against you as evildoers.

That is what makes this verse sting. The talk Peter expects from outsiders, James finds inside the church — brother against brother, over coffee, on the drive home, in a text sent to the one man who will agree with you. It is the world’s weapon picked up by the family.

The dust says it is only talk. But your brother has an Advocate. Christ is at God’s right hand, who also makes intercession for us, and He is speaking for the man you are speaking against. Let His word about your brother outrank yours. If Christ is still praying for that man, you can stop talking about him.

stations.verse: Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?
stations.question: Where have I taken a seat that belongs to God alone and started passing sentence on a brother?
stations.live: When you catch yourself passing sentence on someone this week — at work, at church, at home — stop and say under your breath: ‘Only one is the lawgiver, and it isn’t me.’
body: Nomothetēs joins nomos, law, to tithēmi, to set or lay down. It names the one who lays down the law — not the man who enforces it, but the One who wrote it. James 4:12 is its only New Testament use; the Greek Old Testament has it once, in Psalm 9.

James puts two things in the Lawgiver’s hands: He is able to save and to destroy. No man holds both. You can wound your brother with a sentence, but you cannot save him, and you cannot finally destroy him either. Isaiah names the same seat: Yahweh is our lawgiver. Yahweh is our king. He will save us.

The dust tells you someone has to keep score. Nomothetēs says Someone already does, and He is the One who saves. The Lawgiver came down under His own law, kept it whole, and died for the men who broke it.

practices.title: GET DOWN BEFORE YOU GET UP
practices.body: Before the coffee, before the phone, put your knees on the kitchen floor for two minutes. Not as a ritual to earn the day, but because James 4:10 is a promise, and promises are received low. Say it out loud: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you. Do it on the hard mornings and the easy ones. Then get up and go to work as a man God has promised to lift, not a man who has to hold himself up.

practices.title: NAME THE HOUR AND STAND
practices.body: Temptation keeps a schedule. Know yours — the late night, the drive home, the Friday after payday. When the hour comes, do not debate it. Stand up, change rooms, leave the phone in the truck, call a brother. Then say what James says: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. You are not holding off an enemy who is winning. You are holding ground Christ took at the cross. If you fall, do not lie there arguing with yourself. Confess it, get up, and stand again.

practices.title: WASH HANDS AND HEART BOTH
practices.body: Write two lines on a scrap of paper. On the first, one thing your hands did this week. On the second, one thing your heart has wanted that it should not. Bring both to God and confess them by name: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. Then tear up the paper. It has been washed, and you have no business keeping a record God has thrown away.

practices.title: TAKE DOWN ONE FENCE
practices.body: Find the sin you laugh about and stop laughing. Tell your wife or one trusted brother that the joke is over, and why. Let yourself feel the weight of it for one evening without bracing against it. Then read Psalm 51 slowly, all the way to verse 17. A broken and contrite heart is not something God throws out. It is something He receives. Grief like that is not the end of you. Jesus said those who mourn will be comforted, and He keeps His word.

practices.title: STEP DOWN FROM THE BENCH
practices.body: Pick the brother you have been judging, out loud or in your head. For one week, say nothing against him. Pray for him by name every morning. If you have spoken against him to someone, go back to that person and take it back. Remember whose seat you have been sitting in. Only one is the lawgiver, and He died for that man too. Your brother stands or falls before his own Master, and he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.

title: Down to the Ground
subtitle: from dust to the God who lifts
keyVerse: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

passage.text: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law, but a judge.
Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE LOW PLACE
stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly, out loud if the house allows it, and let it put you on the floor before you answer. Then let the Greek word beneath it show you how far grace reached to get down there with you.
lifeIntro: This week is not about feeling worse so God will think better of you. He has already given more grace. These five practices are ways of getting low enough to receive it, and quiet enough about your brother to stop standing in its way.
lifePulls: Grace does not make a man stand taller before God. It teaches him to kneel, and then it does the lifting he could never do for himself.
prayer: Father, You give more grace, and I come down to receive it. I put myself under You before I try to stand against anything. Keep me standing against the devil, because Christ has already broken his power. Wash my hands from what they did and my heart from what it wanted, by the blood of Jesus. Take the cheap laughter off my sin and give me a grief that leads me home. When the old hour comes, help me stand and not bargain. Shut my mouth when I start to talk my brother down. Remind me that You alone are Lawgiver and Judge, and that the Judge prays for us. Lift me up in Your time, the way You lifted Your Son out of the grave. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You give more grace, and I come down to receive it.
I put myself under You before I try to stand against anything.
Keep me standing against the devil, because Christ has already broken his power.
Wash my hands from what they did and my heart from what it wanted, by the blood of Jesus.
Take the cheap laughter off my sin and give me a grief that leads me home.
When the old hour comes, help me stand and not bargain.
Shut my mouth when I start to talk my brother down.
Remind me that You alone are Lawgiver and Judge, and that the Judge prays for us.
Lift me up in Your time, the way You lifted Your Son out of the grave.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Every command in 4:7–12 stands on 4:6: He gives more grace. So get under God, stand against the devil, and come near to the One who already came near to you. Let the blood wash your hands and your heart. Stop laughing off what ought to break you. Shut your mouth about your brother; the Judge’s seat is taken. Then wait with your head down. God lifts the humbled man. That is a promise, not a mood.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the floor where you finally knelt. Lift them off the sin you have stopped laughing at. Lift them off the brother you have stopped talking down. Lift them off the joke you used to hide behind. Lift them off the hands you held out to be washed. You did not go down there to be left. You went down because God said He would meet you there, and God does not say a thing He will not do.

The dust told you that a man who kneels loses. It told you to keep your feet, keep your guard up, keep your joke ready, keep score on the men around you. It told you that your brother’s failures made you look taller. It lied about all of it. All of that was a man trying to hold himself up off the ground. James took it apart one command at a time — not to crush you, but to empty your hands so that grace would have somewhere to land.

Look at the One who went lower than you ever will. The Son of God stood against the devil in the wilderness and did not fall. He wrapped a towel around His waist and washed feet that would soon run from Him. He was spoken against, condemned by men who had no right to judge Him, and he didn’t open his mouth. He went down into death and was laid in another man’s tomb. He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.

And God did not leave Him there. He reached into the grave and lifted Him out of the dust. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name. That is the lifting James promises you, because you are in Him. The tax collector went home justified. The leper went home clean. You will go home lifted. The risen Christ is at the Father’s right hand right now, speaking for you, and He will not leave a humbled man face-down in the dirt. Go low this week. Stay low before God. The same hand that raised Jesus from the grave is under you, and he will exalt you.
closingVerse: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.
carry: What would you have to stop holding up — your guard, your joke, your verdict on your brother — if you believed God will truly lift the man who goes down before Him?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most kitchens have a calendar on the fridge. Yours probably does. The vet on Thursday. The note on the tractor due on the fifteenth. The boy’s ball games circled in red, the week of vacation blocked out in August, the day the property tax comes due. A man looks at that square of paper and feels the year lying in his hand like a tool he knows how to use.

There is nothing wrong with the calendar. The trouble is the voice behind it. The dust tells you tomorrow is yours — that the season is planned, the money set aside, the work lined up, and all that is left is for you to do it. It tells you the account balance is a fence around your family. It tells you what you have saved will keep, and that a man with enough put back does not need to ask God for daily bread. None of it is true, and some part of you knows it every time you stand at a graveside with your hat in your hands.

The psalmist knew where a man ends up when he leans his weight on what he can count and schedule: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Plans and money come to dust when God is left out of them. So does the man who made them.

James 4:13–5:6 is a hard word, maybe the hardest in the letter. But it is not hard for sport. It pries the calendar and the bank book out of your grip so your hands are free to hold the will of the Lord — which does not rot, does not rust, and does not blow away.

sections.heading: Two Calls to Come Now
pulls: The dust says tomorrow is yours and the money will keep. James says you are a breath on a cold morning, and the only tomorrow worth planning is the one held in the will of the Lord.
paras: This passage opens twice with the same summons: Come now. The first is to the trader with his year planned (4:13–17). The second is to the rich man with his storehouse full and his workers unpaid (5:1–6). The first sins by leaving God out of tomorrow. The second sins by leaving his neighbor out of today. Both are the same sin underneath — a man living as if what he holds were his own.

James writes to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion, and he does not call the rich of chapter five brothers. He speaks against them the way the prophets spoke against proud nations, loud enough for the cheated to hear that God has missed nothing. Read it both ways. If you are the worker, God has heard you. If you hold the money, this is mercy coming while there is still time to answer it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE CALENDAR AND THE MIST
paras: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city, and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.” Nothing in that sentence is a sin on its face. Trade is honest work. Profit feeds families. Planning a year ahead is wisdom. The sin is in who is missing. The man names today, tomorrow, the city, the year, the trade, and the profit — and God is nowhere in the plan. He has drawn up the whole season and left out the One who sends the rain. You know men like that. On some mornings you are one, standing at the counter with your coffee, running the numbers on a year you have not been promised.

Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. You don’t. You did not know the morning the call came about your father, or the day the plant posted the layoffs, or the night the wind took the barn roof. You have been surprised by tomorrow your whole life. Every surprise was a small sermon on this verse, and most of them you slept through. The funeral ends, the casseroles stop coming, and within a month you are planning as if it never happened.

For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away. Think of your breath on a January morning, standing by the truck while it warms up. It is there. It is gone. James is not saying your life is worthless. A breath God gives is a gift. He is saying your life is short and not in your keeping. David prayed, Let me know how frail I am. The man who knows that does not stop planning. He stops planning as if he were God.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: IF THE LORD WILLS
paras: For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.” Look at what James puts first. Not the trip. Not the deal. We will both live. Your next breath is the first thing that hangs on the will of the Lord. The deal comes after. A man who means those words has handed his calendar back to its Owner.

This is not a phrase to tack onto your plans like a rabbit’s foot. It is a man’s whole stance toward tomorrow. He still writes the planting dates on the calendar. He still signs the note at the bank. But he holds all of it with an open hand, because he can say with David, My times are in your hand, and he would rather they be there than in his own.

Then James names the opposite. But now you glory in your boasting. All such boasting is evil. Boasting here is talking about tomorrow as if you owned the deed to it. And he closes with a sentence that will not let you off by nodding along: To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin. You know now. Knowing puts the next step in front of your feet.

Christ is the one Man who ever said If the Lord wills without a crack in it. In the garden, with the cup in front of Him, He prayed, Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. He handed His tomorrow to the Father, and His tomorrow was a cross. Because He did, your tomorrow is not a threat. It is held by the God who raised Him.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ROT, RUST, AND MOTH
pulls: Rust is a witness. Whatever you kept back from the man who earned it or the man who needed it will testify — and the Lord of Armies hears the poorest voice in the field.
paras: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for your miseries that are coming on you. James does not soften this, and you should not either. He sounds like the prophets at the city gate. Weeping and howling is what men do when the judgment they laughed at comes up the road.

Then he walks through the storehouse. Your riches are corrupted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and your silver are corroded. Grain held past its season goes bad. Good coats hung up and never given away feed the moths. Even gold, which does not rust, is spoken of as corroded, as if nothing a man hoards escapes the rot. And the corrosion will be for a testimony against you. The rust on what you kept is evidence. It tells the court what you loved.

Hear what James is not saying. God is not against a full barn. He is the One who richly provides every good thing you have, and He means you to enjoy it. What He will not let you do is trust it, or sit on it while the man next to you goes hungry. You have laid up your treasure in the last days. The last days began when Christ came, and they run until He comes again. To pile up for yourself in these days is to stack hay in a field already marked for the fire.
Jesus said it in plain words: Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume. And He told you why. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WAGES THAT CRY OUT
paras: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out. The rich man’s worst sin is not his fine coat. It is the pay he held back. The law of Moses told Israel to pay a hired man before sundown, lest he cry against you to Yahweh. These men did cry, and the wages cried with them. Money owed to a working man has a voice. Abel’s blood cried from the ground. This cries from the field.

And the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies. The men with the scythes had no lawyer and no one at the courthouse who would listen. They had the Lord of Armies. James sets the largest title for God beside the smallest men in the field. Then he finishes the charge: You have nourished your hearts as in a day of slaughter — fattening like steers the week before the truck comes.

You have condemned and you have murdered the righteous one. He doesn’t resist you. James means the poor man ground down by the powerful. But you cannot read those words without seeing another Righteous One, condemned by rulers and killed, who did not lift a hand to resist. Peter told a crowd they had denied the Holy and Righteous One. Christ let Himself be stripped of everything — His clothes, His justice, His life — and on the cross He paid wages He did not owe. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. That is solid ground for a man with money and for a man without it.

stations.verse: Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away.
stations.question: How would my plans for this year change if I held them as a man whose life is a vapor in God’s hand?
stations.live: Write tomorrow’s plans on a card. Above everything else, write: ‘If the Lord wills, I will live.’ Read it before you leave the house each morning this week, and thank God for the breath.
body: Atmis means vapor. The New Testament uses it twice. Here it is your life. In Acts, Peter quotes the prophet Joel, and the word stands for the smoke of the last days: blood, and fire, and billows of smoke.

Both times the point is the same. It is there, and then it is not. Steam lifts off the coffee in your lunch-pail thermos at the job site; ten seconds later you cannot find it. That is not an insult to your life. It is a measure of it. David asked for that measure: Yahweh, show me my end, what is the measure of my days.

The dust says you have plenty of time. Atmis says you have today, and today was given. But the vapor is not the end of the story for a man in Christ. Your life is hidden with Christ in God, and what is hidden there does not blow away.

stations.verse: But now you glory in your boasting. All such boasting is evil.
stations.question: When I talk about next year at the supper table, do I sound like a man who has only been lent his tomorrow?
stations.live: Listen to yourself this week when you talk about the future. Each time you catch the swagger, stop and say it over again the way James taught you: ‘If the Lord wills.’
body: Alazoneia is the character of the alazōn, the braggart: boastfulness, vainglory, vaunting. It appears twice in the New Testament. The other place is John’s list of what belongs to the world: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.

It is the swagger of a man who talks bigger than what he holds. In James it is a man bragging about a year he has not lived yet. It can sound like ambition. It can sound like a solid plan laid out over coffee at the feed store. Underneath, it is a man claiming what only God owns.

The dust wants you to be the author of your tomorrow, and alazoneia is what that sounds like out loud. Grace hands you something better to boast in — not your plans, but the Lord who holds them. A humbled man says If the Lord wills instead, and sleeps better for it.

stations.verse: Your riches are corrupted and your garments are moth-eaten.
stations.question: What am I keeping for myself that is quietly going bad in storage while someone near me goes without?
stations.live: Walk through your garage, closet, or shop this week. Find one thing of real use you have been keeping that someone else needs now. Give it away by Saturday, and tell no one but God.
body: Sēpō means to make corrupt, to rot. James uses a perfect form — has rotted, has perished — as though the decay is already done when he speaks. This is its only use in the New Testament, and it is a strong word to set beside a man’s savings. In the Greek Old Testament it appears in Psalm 38, of a sick man’s wounds: loathsome and corrupt.

Grain left in the bin too long goes bad. Meat in a dead freezer turns. What a man hoards past its use is not saved. It is spoiled. James looks at the rich man’s storehouse and sees the rot before the man does.

The dust says what you keep, you keep. Sēpō says what you keep for yourself alone is already going bad. But you were bought not with corruptible things, with silver or gold, but with the blood of Christ, and nothing bought with that ever rots.

stations.verse: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies.
stations.question: Whom do I owe — a wage, a bill, a promised payment — that I have been slow to pay because I could get away with it?
stations.live: Pay one bill, debt, or wage you have been sitting on, in full, this week. If you can’t pay it all, call the man and tell him the truth: ‘I owe you, and I mean to make it right.’
body: Aphystereō means to keep back, to withhold. Some manuscripts read a different verb meaning to defraud; either way, the wages were kept from the men who earned them. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Nehemiah 9, where God didn’t withhold manna from His people.

God fed a grumbling people in the wilderness, morning after morning, and held nothing back. The rich man held back from honest workers what he plainly owed. Late pay, a shorted check, a bill you let ride because the man can’t afford to chase you — that is this word.

The dust says you got the better end of the deal. Aphystereō says the deal is on the record. And look at God’s way with you. He has never held back what He promised. He who didn’t spare his own Son, will He hold back anything you need?

stations.verse: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies.
stations.question: When I am the one who has been cheated, do I trust that the Lord of Armies has heard the cry?
stations.live: If someone has cheated you, write it down and hand it to God by name: ‘The Lord of Armies has heard this. I will not take my own revenge. I leave it with Him.’
body: Sabaōth is a Hebrew word carried over in Greek letters. It means hosts, or armies. The Greek Old Testament keeps it chiefly in Isaiah, and the New Testament has it twice: here, and where Paul quotes Isaiah in Romans 9.

Notice where James sets the title. Not over a battlefield or a throne room, but over a hayfield where men were cheated out of a day’s pay. The Lord of every army in heaven has bent His ear to the field hand. No man is too small to be heard by Him, and no rich man is too big to answer to Him.

The dust tells a cheated man to get even or give up. Sabaōth says neither. Paul uses the name to say God kept His people when all looked lost: Unless the Lord of Armies had left us a seed. The One who kept the seed will keep you.

practices.title: PUT GOD ON THE CALENDAR
practices.body: Take the calendar off the fridge, or open the one you carry. Look at the next month. Across the top, write the words of 4:15: If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that. Do it in ink, where your wife and children will see it. Then pray through the month square by square. Do not ask God to bless your plans as if He were signing off on them. Hand them to Him, and ask Him to change whatever He wants changed.

practices.title: COUNT YOUR DAYS
practices.body: Psalm 90 asks God to teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom. Do the arithmetic once this week. The same psalm gives a man seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years. Set your age against that and look at what is left. Do not do it to scare yourself. Do it so today matters, and so you stop putting off the good you already know to do. James says that kind of putting off is sin. Christ has forgiven it. Go do it.

practices.title: AUDIT THE STOREHOUSE
practices.body: Walk through what you own: the shop, the closet, the deep freezer, the account you never touch. At each stop ask one question — is this being used, or is it rotting? Pick one thing that is only being kept. Give it, or sell it and give the money, or put it to work for someone in need before the week is out. Let your hands open on purpose. A man whose Savior gave everything for him can afford to let go of a chest freezer’s worth of anything.

practices.title: PAY WHAT YOU OWE
practices.body: Make a list of what you owe — wages, bills, a loan from a friend, a fair price you haggled down too far. Pay one of them this week, early if you can. If anyone works for you, pay him on time and pay him in full. The Lord of Armies hears the cry of the man who gets shorted. Let Him hear that man thank God for you instead. You were paid in full at the cross. Pay your own debts like a man who knows it.

practices.title: LAY UP WHERE MOTH CAN’T REACH
practices.body: Jesus told you where to keep treasure: lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume. Pick one place to give this month that will outlast you — your church, a widow’s heating bill, a missionary you know by name. Give an amount you will feel. Then thank Christ, who though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor. Every dollar you give this way is a small echo of what He did for you, and none of it will rot.

title: Mist and Moth
subtitle: from dust to the will of the Lord
keyVerse: For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.

passage.text: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city, and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.”
Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away.
For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.”
But now you glory in your boasting. All such boasting is evil.
To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.
Come now, you rich, weep and howl for your miseries that are coming on you.
Your riches are corrupted and your garments are moth-eaten.
Your gold and your silver are corroded, and their corrosion will be for a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up your treasure in the last days.
Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you have kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries of those who reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Armies.
You have lived in luxury on the earth, and taken your pleasure. You have nourished your hearts as in a day of slaughter.
You have condemned and you have murdered the righteous one. He doesn’t resist you.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON TOMORROW AND TREASURE
stationsIntro: These five words are hard ones: vapor, bragging, rot, wages held back, and the Lord of Armies. Read each verse slowly, then let the word show you what God sees in your plans and your purse — and what He has already done about it in Christ.
lifeIntro: Your tomorrow and your treasure were never yours to hold. God lent you both, and He gave His Son before He asked you for anything. These five practices loosen your grip and put both back in the hands of the One who gave them.
lifePulls: Your life is a breath and your money is already rusting. Neither is bad news for a man whose tomorrow is held in the will of the Lord and whose treasure is laid up in Christ.
prayer: Father, my life is a vapor, and every breath I take is Yours. Forgive me for planning my tomorrows as if I held the deed to them. Teach me to say, and mean, If the Lord wills. Show me what I am keeping that is going to rot, and loosen my grip on it. Make me quick to pay what I owe and glad to give what I can. Where I have held back what was owed, give me the courage to make it right this week. Thank You that You hear the cry of the cheated man in the field. Thank You that Christ became poor so that I could be made rich in Him. Hold my days in Your hand, and keep me until the day He comes again. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, my life is a vapor, and every breath I take is Yours.
Forgive me for planning my tomorrows as if I held the deed to them.
Teach me to say, and mean, If the Lord wills.
Show me what I am keeping that is going to rot, and loosen my grip on it.
Make me quick to pay what I owe and glad to give what I can.
Where I have held back what was owed, give me the courage to make it right this week.
Thank You that You hear the cry of the cheated man in the field.
Thank You that Christ became poor so that I could be made rich in Him.
Hold my days in Your hand, and keep me until the day He comes again.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: You do not own tomorrow, and your money will not keep. Your life is a vapor, and what you hoard is already rusting. So say it and mean it: if the Lord wills. Pay what you owe. Give what is only being kept. The Lord of Armies hears the cry of the cheated, and Christ became poor to make you rich. Put your treasure where He is.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the One who holds tomorrow. The calendar does not hold it. The bank does not hold it. The tools in the shop and the coat in the closet do not hold it. The plans you made without asking do not hold it, and the bills you let ride will not hold it for you. The Lord holds it — the Lord whose will gives you your next breath, and whose ear is bent low toward the field.

The dust told you tomorrow was yours and money would keep. Tomorrow never was yours, and money never could keep. Your days are a vapor, and everything you hoard is already on its way to rust. That is hard to hear. But it is mercy to hear it now, while it is still today, while your hands can still open and your debts can still be paid. God did not send James to sneer at you. He sent him to wake you before the fire. A God who warns is a God who still means to save.

Look at the Righteous One. He was rich beyond counting, and for your sakes he became poor. The Son of Man has no place to lay his head, He said. They took His clothes and cast lots for them. He was condemned and killed, and He did not resist. In the garden He prayed what you find so hard to pray: not my will, but yours, be done. He gave His tomorrow to the Father, and the Father answered with an empty tomb and a life that can never be lost again.

So your tomorrow is not a threat, and your treasure in Him is not lost. The One who holds your days walked out of the grave, and He has gone to prepare a place for you. This Jesus will come back the same way He went, and on that day the cheated man in the field and the rich man who repented will stand side by side, both bought by the same blood. What is laid up in Him does not rot, does not rust, and does not blow away. Plan your week. Hold it loose. Pay your men. Give with an open hand. And say it every morning, because it is true: if the Lord wills, you will live — and in Christ, you will live forever.
closingVerse: For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.
carry: What would change in your plans and your spending this week if you believed your next breath hangs on the will of the Lord and your only lasting treasure is already in Christ?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There is a lie the dust tells a waiting man, and it tells it slowly. It does not say God is gone. It says God is late. The money you were owed has not come. The ground you planted in April is still bare in June. Your son has not called. The pain in your back has not let up, and the man who cheated you on the last job is driving a new truck. You pray about it on the drive in every morning, and every evening the answer is the same as yesterday. Nothing moves. A man who waits long enough with nothing moving starts to believe that nothing is coming.

Then the lie goes to work on your hands and your mouth. If nothing is coming, take what you can get now. If nothing is coming, somebody ought to pay for the wait, and the nearest somebody is the person beside you — your wife, your brother, the men on your crew. So you grumble. And if nothing is coming, your word needs propping up, so you add the oath. I swear. I promise you. On my mother’s grave. Your plain yes has stopped carrying weight, even with you.

That is a soul face-down in the dust, and Psalm 119:25 gives him words to pray: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) James answers with a farmer, a field, and a rain that has never once failed to come in its season. The Lord is coming. The waiting is not empty. It has an end, and the end has a name.

sections.heading: After the Rich, a Word to the Brothers
pulls: The dust says God is late and nothing is coming. James says the Lord is coming, the Judge is already at the door, and a man who knows the rain is promised can put down his fists and wait.
paras: The verses just before these were hard words aimed at rich men who held back the wages of the men who mowed their fields and fattened themselves while those men cried out (5:1–6). Then James turns. Be patient therefore, brothers. That word therefore ties the two halves together. The men he speaks to now are the ones on the short end of the deal — the cheated, the overlooked, the believers scattered among the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion (1:1).

James does not promise them the wrong will be set right by Friday. He does not tell them to take matters into their own hands. He points them to the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ, the one bodily return of the One who was taken up into the sky and will come back in the same way (Acts 1:11). Everything in these six verses hangs on that event: the farmer’s patience, the steady heart, the closed mouth, the plain yes. Read 5:7–12 aloud before you go on. It takes less than a minute, and it will show you what kind of man waits well.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE FARMER AND THE RAIN
paras: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. The patience James asks for is not a mood. It has an until fastened to the end of it. A man can wait a long time for something he knows is coming. What breaks him is waiting for nothing.

So James hands you a farmer. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain. Every man who has put seed in the ground knows the shape of this. You plow, you plant, you mend the fence. Then you wait on what you cannot make. No farmer ever pulled rain out of the sky by worrying at it. His patience rests on a promise older than his field: God told Israel He would give the rain for your land in its season, the early rain and the latter rain (Deuteronomy 11:14). The farmer waits because the rain has been promised, not because he is a patient sort of man.

Notice what James calls the crop. Precious. The farmer is not waiting on scraps, and neither is the Lord. James told you in the first chapter that God gave birth to us by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures (1:18). You are part of the crop. The Lord Jesus bled on the cross to buy that harvest, rose from the grave to guarantee it, and is coming back to bring it in. He has been more patient over His field than you have ever been over yours.
So the patience asked of you is an answer to grace, not a wage you earn. You do not earn the rain by waiting well. The rain is promised, so you wait.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: HEARTS SET FAST
paras: You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand. The Lord who sends the rain also steadies the heart that waits for it. Then James tells you where patience lives. Not in the jaw. In the heart. The word means to set fast, the way you set a post in concrete so the wind cannot work it loose.

The reason is the same as before: the coming of the Lord is at hand. That does not hand you a date. James gave no timeline, and no one since has been given one. It tells you that the next great event on God’s calendar is Christ Himself, coming once, bodily, in glory, to raise the dead, judge the living and the dead, and make all things new. Nothing else has to be finished first for that day to be near. The hour is His. The nearness is yours to live in this morning.

Then James puts his finger on the first thing that leaks out of a man who has waited too long. Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged. Hard seasons turn men on each other. You come home tired and the first sharp word goes to your wife. The crew hears about it next. The brother in the next pew gets the side comment.

Behold, the judge stands at the door. That is meant to sober you, not to scare you off. The Judge at the door is the same Jesus who stood in your place and took the judgment you were owed. He has heard every word said in your kitchen. He also bled for the worst of them. A man who knows that can shut his mouth and wait.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE PROPHETS AND JOB
pulls: The point of Job is not Job’s grit. It is God’s heart. James sends you to the outcome so you will see what the Lord was all along — full of compassion and mercy, even in the ash.
paras: Take, brothers, for an example of suffering and of perseverance, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. James does not send you to men who had it easy. He sends you to men who spoke for God and paid for it. Jeremiah was let down with cords into a dungeon and sank in the mire (Jeremiah 38:6). That suffering was not a sign that God had left them. It came because they belonged to Him.

Behold, we call them blessed who endured. Look back at any of them and the word you reach for is blessed. Not one of them felt blessed in the mud. Blessing is a verdict God gives, and it is read best from the end of the story.

Then James names the man every sufferer knows. You have heard of the perseverance of Job, and have seen the Lord in the outcome. Job lost his herds, his children, and his health in a short stretch of days. He argued. He cursed the day of his birth (Job 3:1). He did not endure quietly. But God never let go of him. In the end Yahweh blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning (Job 42:12).

And here is what James wants you to see in the outcome: how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy. The point of Job is not Job’s grit. It is God’s heart. The fullest look at that heart is not Job’s restored herds. It is the cross, where the Son endured the worst, and the empty tomb, where the Father showed how it came out. Jesus endured the cross, despising its shame (Hebrews 12:2), and the outcome was life. Your trouble has an outcome too, and the Lord who is full of compassion is the One writing it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: LET YOUR YES BE YES
paras: But above all things, my brothers, don’t swear— not by heaven, or by the earth, or by any other oath. Begin here: God’s word has never once failed you. A man who doubts the Lord is coming starts propping himself up, and one of the first things he props is his word.

Jesus had already exposed the game. Men swore by the temple and by the gold of the temple, by the altar and by the gift on it, and argued over which oaths bound them (Matthew 23:16–22). The more they swore, the cheaper their plain word got. So Jesus said don’t swear at all (Matthew 5:34), and James says the same. This is not a ruling against the witness stand. Scripture shows God Himself swearing an oath. The target is the everyday oath a man adds because his yes has stopped holding.

Let your “yes” be “yes”, and your “no”, “no”, so that you don’t fall into hypocrisy. A short yes, kept, is honest. A long oath stacked on a weak yes is a mask, and James calls it hypocrisy. The man who wears it ends up with two kinds of words — the ones he swears to and the ones he does not — and his wife and children learn to sort them.

Here is the grace under the command. When God made His promise to Abraham, since he could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself (Hebrews 6:13). His word never needed help. You did. He added the oath so a man of dust would have something sure to stand on. And every promise of God has its yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), sealed at the cross and the empty tomb. A man standing on that much yes can afford to let his own be short — and keep it.

stations.verse: Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain.
stations.question: When my waiting runs long, do I wait like a farmer who knows the rain is promised?
stations.gloss: to be long-tempered; to bear patiently
stations.live: Name the one wait that has made you short with people — the payment, the diagnosis, the son. Each time it flares this week, say: ‘The Lord has been patient with me. I can wait on Him.’
body: Makrothymeō comes from a word meaning long-tempered. A short temper burns hot and quick. A long one holds. The verb shows up in nine verses of the New Testament, and in some of the weightiest of them God is the one being patient.

Peter says the Lord is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish (2 Peter 3:9). The Lord’s patience is the reason the last day has not come yet, and the reason you were not lost before He found you. James asks you to be long-tempered toward a world that wrongs you because God has been long-tempered toward you. Abraham waited the same way: having patiently endured, he obtained the promise (Hebrews 6:15).
The dust says a short fuse is just how you are built. Makrothymeō says your fuse can grow long, because God’s fuse has been long with you, and the Lord you wait for is not slow about His promise.

stations.verse: You also be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
stations.question: Is my heart set fast on the coming of the Lord, even through a long week of bad reports?
stations.gloss: to fix firmly; to set fast; to establish
stations.live: Each morning this week, before the news or the phone, say one sentence out loud at the kitchen table: ‘The coming of the Lord is at hand. The Lord will set my heart fast today.’
body: Stērizō means to fix, to set fast, to make firm. Luke uses it of Jesus on the road: he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). His face was set like a survey stake at the corner of a lot, pointed at the cross, and nothing on the road worked it loose.

That is the first thing to know about a steady heart. Christ set His face for you before you ever set your heart on Him. And God is the one who does the setting: He will perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle you (1 Peter 5:10). Jesus told Peter, I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail (Luke 22:32). When James says establish your hearts, you obey by leaning your whole weight on what God has already fixed in place.
The dust wants your heart loose, so every wind can rock it. Stērizō drives it down into the coming of the Lord, where the ground does not move.

stations.verse: Take, brothers, for an example of suffering and of perseverance, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
stations.question: Do I read the hardship I carry for doing right as proof that God has left me?
stations.live: Write down one hardship you are carrying because you did the right thing. Under it write the name of one prophet, then the name of Jesus. Read that list when the hardship bites.
body: Kakopatheia means distress, affliction — hardship a man has to carry. It is built on a word for one who suffers. This verse is the only place it appears in the New Testament. James reached for a rare word to name a common thing.

He sets it beside perseverance and hangs both on the prophets. Those men did not suffer because they were far from God. They suffered because they spoke in His name. Their hardship was the cost of belonging to Him. Yours may be the same: the cost of telling the truth on the job, of keeping your vows when it would be easier not to, of turning down the easy money.

The dust says suffering means you are on your own. Kakopatheia puts you in company. The prophets walked this road ahead of you, and Christ walked it all the way to the cross so you would never walk it alone.

stations.verse: Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the perseverance of Job, and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
stations.question: When I look back at the hardest season I have come through, do I see the Lord who is full of compassion and mercy?
stations.live: Tell one man this week about a hard season you came through and where you now see the Lord’s compassion in how it came out. Close by saying: ‘The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.’
body: Polysplanchnos joins polys to splanchnon, and it means very pitiful in the old sense — not pitiable, but full of pity. This verse is its only appearance in the New Testament, and James spends it on one subject: what the Lord is.

And he says it about the Lord in Job’s story, a story full of ash, sores, and graves. The compassion was there the whole time, under the silence. It came into plain view in the outcome. That is where James tells you to look: not only at the middle of the story, where you are standing, but at the end the Lord is bringing. The cross looked like the end of mercy. Three days later it was the proof of it.
The dust says God is hard, and you have to wring kindness out of Him. Polysplanchnos says His compassion is not thin and not grudging. It is full.

stations.verse: But above all things, my brothers, don’t swear— not by heaven, or by the earth, or by any other oath; but let your “yes” be “yes”, and your “no”, “no”, so that you don’t fall into hypocrisy.
stations.question: Does my plain yes still carry weight with the people closest to me?
stations.gloss: to swear; to affirm by oath
stations.live: For one week, drop every ‘I swear’ and ‘I promise you’ from your speech. Say yes or no, and then do it. Where you cannot do it, say so plainly and early.
body: Omnymi means to swear, to affirm by oath. It appears in twenty verses of the New Testament, and several of them have God as the one who swears: to Abraham (Hebrews 6:13), to David (Acts 2:30), and to the Son as a priest forever (Hebrews 7:21).

Others are darker. In the courtyard on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter began to curse and to swear that he did not know Him (Matthew 26:74). The oath propped up a lie. The rooster crowed. The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and after the resurrection He restored him by the sea. The oath could not hold Peter up. Christ did, and He sent him back out with a plain word to feed the sheep.
The dust says your word needs more weight. Omnymi shows you where the weight already is. God swore by Himself so you would have a sure hope. Stand on His oath, and your own yes can be short.

practices.title: NAME THE FIELD YOU ARE WAITING ON
practices.body: Write down the one thing you have waited on longest — the debt, the diagnosis, the prodigal, the job that never opens up. Next to it write the coming of the Lord is at hand. You have done the plowing. You cannot make the rain. Pray over that field each morning, and then leave it with the One who sends rain in its season. A farmer does not dig up the seed every day to see whether it is growing.

practices.title: SET THE POST BEFORE THE WIND
practices.body: A post is set before the storm, not during it. Before your day starts, set your heart on one fact: Christ is coming back, once, bodily, in glory. Read Acts 1:11 aloud over your coffee. Then go to work with that settled. When the wind hits at ten in the morning — the bad call, the blown estimate — you will not be digging the hole for the post in the middle of the storm.

practices.title: SHUT THE GRUMBLE AT THE DOOR
practices.body: Grumbling runs downhill toward the people nearest you. This week, when the complaint rises against your wife, your crew, or a brother at church, stop at the door of your mouth and remember who stands at the other door. Behold, the judge stands at the door. He bore the judgment for you. Let that close your mouth, and then go say one kind word to the person you were about to blame.

practices.title: TAKE JOB OFF THE SHELF
practices.body: Read Job 1, Job 2, and Job 42 in one sitting this week. Watch how much Job lost and how little he understood. Then watch the end. James says you have seen the Lord in the outcome. Write one line about where your own story stands right now, and one line about the Lord’s heart toward you that the outcome will prove. Then read Hebrews 12:2 and set Job’s outcome beside Christ’s. The Lord who raised His Son is not finished with you.

practices.title: KEEP YOUR WORD SHORT AND KEPT
practices.body: Strip the oaths out of your speech — I swear, I promise you, on my life. Then do the harder part: keep the plain yes. If you told your son Saturday, it is Saturday. If you said no to the side deal, it stays no. God swore by Himself to give you a sure hope. Let a man under that much promise say little and mean every word of it.

title: The Farmer’s Rain
subtitle: from dust to the Lord who is coming
keyVerse: Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the perseverance of Job, and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

Don’t grumble, brothers, against one another, so that you won’t be judged. Behold, the judge stands at the door.
