Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the perseverance of Job, and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
But above all things, my brothers, don’t swear— not by heaven, or by the earth, or by any other oath; but let your “yes” be “yes”, and your “no”, “no”, so that you don’t fall into hypocrisy.

stationsIntro: Five words carry these six verses. Read each verse slowly, answer the question as yourself and not as the man you wish you were, and let the Greek send you back into the text rather than past it.
lifeIntro: The Lord is coming, and He has been long-tempered with you the whole time you waited. Let His coming set the pace of your waiting, your words, and your home. Five practices, all of them out of six verses.
lifePulls: The farmer does not make the rain. He plants, he waits, and he keeps his hands off his neighbor. The Lord is coming, and that is enough to make a man patient, steady, quiet, and plain.
prayer: Father, You have promised that the Lord Jesus is coming, and You do not lie. You were long-tempered with me when I was far from You, and You are patient with me still. Set my heart fast on His coming, the way He set His face toward the cross for me. Keep my mouth from grumbling against my wife, my brothers, and the men I work beside. When I suffer, let me see the prophets ahead of me and Christ ahead of them. Show me Your compassion and mercy in the end You are writing for my life. Strip the oaths out of my speech and make my yes a yes I keep. Come, Lord Jesus. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You have promised that the Lord Jesus is coming, and You do not lie.
You were long-tempered with me when I was far from You, and You are patient with me still.
Set my heart fast on His coming, the way He set His face toward the cross for me.
Keep my mouth from grumbling against my wife, my brothers, and the men I work beside.
When I suffer, let me see the prophets ahead of me and Christ ahead of them.
Show me Your compassion and mercy in the end You are writing for my life.
Strip the oaths out of my speech and make my yes a yes I keep.
Come, Lord Jesus.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: James turns from the rich men to the brothers they cheated and tells them to wait like a farmer. The rain is promised. The Lord is coming, once and bodily, and the Judge already stands at the door — the same Judge who was judged for you. So set your heart fast, stop grumbling at the people beside you, look at the prophets and at Job, and let your yes be yes. The waiting is not empty.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, the way a farmer lifts his toward the west in a dry June. Look past the bare field. Look past the empty mailbox. Look past the long silence where an answer ought to be. Look to the door where the Judge stands. Look to the Lord who was taken up into the sky and will come back in the same way. The dust told you God is late. He is not late. He is long-tempered, and His patience is the reason you were found before the end came.

You did not make the rain, and you were never asked to. You were asked to wait for it. The prophets waited in dungeons and in hiding, and we call them blessed who endured. Job waited in the ash while his friends got it wrong, and at the end the Lord gave him more than he had at the start. None of them held on by his own strength. They were held. The same hands hold you now — through the long dry stretch, the hospital hallway, the lean year, the night you cannot sleep for the money. You are not waiting alone, and you are not waiting for nothing.

So look at the outcome you can already see. Christ suffered more than any prophet, was laid in a tomb sealed with a stone, and walked out of it alive. That outcome tells you what the Lord is like. He is full of compassion and mercy. He did not leave His Son in the grave, and He will not leave you in the dust. The One who stands at the door as Judge is the One who stood in your place and was judged. When He opens that door, it will not be to throw you out. It will be to bring you in.

So set your heart fast. Keep your mouth gentle toward your brother and your yes plain before God. Plant, mend, wait. The Lord Jesus is coming back, once and in His own body, to raise the dead and gather His harvest, and you are part of the crop He bled to buy. The early rain and the late rain have come every year since the promise was made, and the coming of the Lord will not fail either. He is at hand, and He will find you.
closingVerse: Behold, we call them blessed who endured. You have heard of the perseverance of Job, and have seen the Lord in the outcome, and how the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.
carry: What field have you been standing over, angry at the sky, when the Lord who is coming would have you plant, wait, and keep your mouth gentle toward the people beside you?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust tells a hurting man to keep it to himself. You do not call anybody when your back gives out or the test comes back wrong. You do not tell the brothers about the second drink, or the screen you went back to at midnight, or the grudge you have nursed against your father for twenty years. You handle it. You grit your teeth through the pain and carry the sin like a stone in your pocket, and nobody at church needs to know about either one. The pain stays private, the sin stays buried, and you call that strength.

Then the dust tells you prayer is for other men. Elijah could pray and shut the sky. You pray and the ceiling stays where it is. Men like that were cut from different stuff. So you pray short and seldom, the way a man tosses a coin in a fountain, and you expect about as much back. And when a brother drifts — stops coming on Sunday, goes cold, starts living like he never heard of Christ — the dust tells you that is his business. Let him go. He knew better. You have enough trouble of your own.

That is a soul flattened in the dust, and Psalm 119:25 is his prayer: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) James ends his letter by pulling down every one of those lies. Pray. Call the elders. Confess. Elijah was a man made of your dust. And go after the brother who wandered, because Someone came after you.

sections.heading: A Letter That Ends with a Rescue
pulls: The dust tells you to carry the pain alone, hide the sin, and let the wandering brother go. James ends his letter with men praying, confessing, and walking out the door after a brother to bring him home.
paras: Paul’s letters usually close with greetings and a blessing. James stops cold. His last sentence is about a sinner turned back from the error of his way, and then the letter is over. That is not a loose end. It is the whole letter pressed down into a single act, one brother walking out to bring another home. James began with Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations (1:2). He ends with brothers carrying one another through those trials to the finish.

These eight verses gather up what James has said since the first chapter. The trials of 1:2 come back as suffering and sickness. The tongue of chapter 3 comes back as prayer, praise, and confession. The grace of 4:6 comes back as sins forgiven and covered. The Lord who is coming in 5:7 is still near. Read 5:13–20 through once before you start, and watch how often prayer shows up. It is in six of the eight verses. None of this is new teaching. It is the whole letter turned into a way for brothers to live together.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: CALL FOR THE ELDERS
paras: Before James says a word about prayer, settle who is listening. You have a Father who hears. Christ sits at the right hand of God, and he lives forever to make intercession for those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25). Your prayer is not a shout into an empty sky. It goes up beside His.

Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises. James covers the whole week in two lines. Bad day or good day, turn your face toward God. The man who only prays in trouble treats God like a tow truck. The man who only sings when things go well has a God for fair weather. James wants your mouth open to Him in every season.

Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. Notice who moves first. The sick man calls. A man laid up in bed has to admit he is laid up, and that comes hard to men who measure themselves by what their hands can do. James tells you to pick up the phone anyway. Then the elders come to you, and they pray over you.

The oil is not medicine and it is not magic. It is done in the name of the Lord, and the name carries the weight. Whatever comfort the oil brings, the power is not in the bottle. It is in the One the elders call on. The church was never meant to be a place where men suffer behind closed doors. It is a body, and when one part is laid low, the rest of the body comes to the bed.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE LORD WILL RAISE HIM UP
paras: And the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. Read this verse with care, because careless readings of it have crushed men. The faith here is faith in the Lord, not faith in an outcome. And the one who does the raising is the Lord — not the elders, and not the strength of anyone’s believing.

Sometimes He raises a sick man from his bed in a week, and the man goes back to work. Sometimes He does not, and the man dies trusting Him. That is not a failed prayer. Paul wrote, I left Trophimus at Miletus sick (2 Timothy 4:20). Paul himself asked for relief and was told My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). Every believer the Lord does not raise from the bed now, He will raise from the grave on the last day. No prayer offered in His name is wasted. The elders pray, and they leave the answer with Him. So do you.

If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven. James sets the deeper healing right beside the first. Not every sickness comes from a sin, and James says if. But the Lord who raises bodies also forgives sinners, and He does it at the cross, where Jesus bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).

So James goes on: Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. Confession does not pay for the sin. Christ paid. Confession drags it into the light, where your brother can pray and where the dark loses its grip. The stone in your pocket gets lighter when another man knows it is there. Your brother is not your priest. He is a sinner under the same blood, praying beside you.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ELIJAH ON HIS KNEES
pulls: Elijah was not a different kind of man. He ran, he hid, he asked to die. The power was never in the man on his knees. It was in the God who said He would send rain and sent it.
paras: The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective. Do not hear the word righteous and count yourself out. James has already told you how a man is counted righteous: Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him as righteousness (2:23). Your standing before God is Christ’s righteousness, given to you. And the one fully righteous man whose prayer never fails is Jesus Himself, praying for you today.

Then James reaches for Elijah, the prophet who shut the sky, and says the last thing you expect. Elijah was a man with a nature like ours. Not a different kind of man. The same dust. The same fear. After the fire fell on Carmel, Elijah ran for his life, sat down under a juniper tree, and asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4). That is the man James puts in front of you.

He prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it didn’t rain on the earth for three years and six months. Then: He prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit. On top of Carmel Elijah put his face between his knees (1 Kings 18:42), and he sent his servant to look toward the sea seven times before a cloud the size of a man’s hand came up. That was not a speech. It was a man bent low, asking and looking and asking again.

The power was never in Elijah. It was in the God who had said He would send rain and then sent it. Prayer is a man of dust asking the God who keeps His word to do what He said. You can do that. The same God hears you, and Christ has opened the way in.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: TURN HIM BACK
paras: Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back. James finishes with a man drifting. Not a man outside the church. Any among you. Wandering seldom starts with a slammed door. It starts with a missed Sunday, a friendship gone cool, a sin he quits fighting and starts defending. Maybe he got hurt by someone in the church and never said so. One day he is far off, and nobody saw him go.

James does not say leave him be. He says someone turns him back, and that someone can be you. Not because you are better than he is. You were a wanderer too: you were going astray like sheep; but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls (1 Peter 2:25). Jesus came to seek and to save that which was lost (Luke 19:10), and He came for you first. Every rescue you have a hand in is a small copy of His.

He who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins. Read it with care. The soul saved from death is the wanderer’s. The sins covered are his, and they are covered the only way sins are ever covered — by the blood of Christ, received as the man turns back in repentance. You earn nothing by going. You are the hand on the rope. Christ is the One who saves.

So go. Call him. Drive out to his place. Sit at his table. Bring your own story of wandering. Say the hard thing gently and the true thing plainly. The Shepherd who brought you home is still out looking, and He is glad to use a brother’s voice.

stations.verse: And the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
stations.question: When I am worn down in body, will I let the elders of my church carry me to the Lord in prayer?
stations.gloss: to work; to grow weary; to be sick
stations.live: If you are sick or worn down, call one elder or one brother this week and ask him to pray over you in person. Say it plainly: ‘I am laid low. Come and pray for me.’
body: Kamnō first means to work. Then it means what long work does to a man: to grow weary. Then it comes to mean to be sick. The word itself follows a man off the job site, onto the couch, and into the bed. It appears only twice in the New Testament.

The other place is Hebrews 12:3: consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don’t grow weary. The weary man is pointed to Jesus. James points the sick man to the Lord who raises up. In neither place is the worn-out man told to try harder. He is told where to look, and who to call.

The dust says a tired, sick man is useless and ought to keep quiet. Kamnō says the Lord knows exactly how far down a body can go, and He is the One who will raise him up. He raised His Son, and He will raise you.

stations.verse: Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.
stations.question: Do I want healing badly enough to confess my sin to a brother?
stations.live: Choose one brother you trust and tell him the sin you have carried alone. Ask him to pray for you, and pray for him in return. Close with: ‘By His wounds I am healed.’
body: Iaomai means to heal. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew word for healing, and Luke uses it again and again for what Jesus did with His hands: power came out of him and healed them all (Luke 6:19). He healed with a word and with a touch. It appears in twenty-six verses of the New Testament.

The word also reaches past the body. Peter uses it of the deepest healing there is: You were healed by his wounds (1 Peter 2:24). James sets healing right after confession. The wound that festers in the dark gets cleaned in the light, among brothers, under the blood of Christ. The healing does not come from the telling. It comes from the Savior the telling brings you back to.
The dust says hide it and it will heal on its own. Iaomai says hidden sin does not heal. Confessed sin meets a Savior already wounded for it. Bring it out, and let the Healer work.

stations.verse: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it didn’t rain on the earth for three years and six months.
stations.question: Have I told myself that prayer works only for stronger, holier men than me?
stations.gloss: of like nature; of like feelings
stations.live: Name one thing you quit praying about because you decided God would not move for a man like you. Pray for it every day this week: ‘Elijah was a man like me. Hear me too.’
body: Homoiopathēs is built from homoios and paschō, and it means of like feelings — a man who feels what you feel and suffers what you suffer. It appears twice in the New Testament.

At Lystra the crowd tried to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods. The two men tore their clothes and cried out that they were men of like passions with you (Acts 14:15). James says the same of Elijah. The man who shut the sky was made of your dust. And the Christ who hears you took on that same dust Himself. He was in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), so He knows from the inside what it is to be a man on his knees.
The dust says prayer belongs to giants. Homoiopathēs says Elijah was no giant. The God who heard him is the God who hears you. Pray like a man who is heard.

stations.verse: Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back.
stations.question: Is there a brother I have watched drift from the truth and said nothing to, because it felt like his business?
stations.gloss: to lead astray; to wander; to go astray
stations.live: Write the name of one man who has drifted. Before Sunday, call him or knock on his door. Do not lecture. Say: ‘I miss you, brother. I came to bring you home.’
body: Planaō means to cause to wander or to lead astray, and in the passive, to go astray. It is a word for sheep: Jesus speaks of the one that goes astray while the ninety-nine stay put (Matthew 18:12). It appears in thirty-seven verses of the New Testament, often of deception.

James used it once before: Don’t be deceived, my beloved brothers (1:16). The letter opens with a warning not to wander and closes with a plan for when someone does. A drifting man is usually deceived first. He does not think he is leaving. He thinks he is resting. That is why he needs a brother who will tell him the truth.

The dust says the wanderer chose his road, so leave him on it. Planaō says he is a sheep, and sheep need a shepherd. You were one. Christ came for you, and He did not wait for you to find your own way back.

stations.verse: Let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
stations.question: Am I still trying to cover my sins myself with silence and good behavior?
stations.gloss: to cover; to hide from view
stations.live: Name the sin you have been covering with silence or busyness. Bring it to God in plain words, and then thank Him out loud: ‘You have covered all my sin in Christ.’
body: Kalyptō means to cover, and in the Greek Old Testament it almost always stands for the Hebrew word to cover. It is used of the forgiveness of sins, as in the psalm: You have covered all their sin (Psalm 85:2). It appears in seven verses of the New Testament. Peter uses it the same way: love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8).

James says the sins covered are a multitude. The man who goes after the wanderer does not cover them with his own goodness. They are covered by the blood of Christ, applied as the wanderer turns back to Him. Your part is the walk to his door. Christ’s part is the cross, and His part is finished.
The dust tells you to cover sin with silence. That kind of cover rots whatever is under it. Kalyptō points you to the cover God supplies, and it holds.

practices.title: PRAY IN BOTH KINDS OF WEATHER
practices.body: Suffering? Pray. Cheerful? Sing. This week, every time something goes wrong, say one short prayer before you say anything else. Every time something goes right, say one line of thanks or sing one verse of a hymn in the truck. You have a Savior who lives forever to make intercession. Let your prayers in fair weather and foul go up beside His, and watch how much of your day turns out to be His.

practices.title: MAKE THE CALL
practices.body: If you are sick, worn down, or facing surgery, call the elders of your church this week. Ask them to come and pray over you in the name of the Lord. Do not wait until it is worse, and do not tell yourself you are a bother. This is what the body is for, and the Lord who raises up is the One they will call on. If you are an elder, go when you are called.

practices.title: CONFESS TO ONE BROTHER
practices.body: Pick one man you trust. Tell him the sin you have been carrying alone — the phone, the bottle, the grudge, the money. You are not telling him to earn forgiveness; Christ has already paid for it. You are telling him so the dark loses its hold and he can pray for you. Then listen while he does the same, and pray for him.

practices.title: PRAY ONE ELIJAH PRAYER
practices.body: Choose one request you dropped because it seemed too big — a son’s salvation, a marriage gone cold, a church that has lost its way. Pray for it every day this week, on your knees if your knees allow. Write the request on a card and keep it in your wallet, so you see it every time you pay for something. Elijah sent his servant to look seven times. Keep looking. The same God hears you, and Christ has opened the way in.

practices.title: GO GET YOUR BROTHER
practices.body: Write down the name of one man who used to stand beside you and does not anymore. Call him, or drive to his place. Do not open with what he did wrong. Open with the fact that you miss him and that Christ is still calling him home. Tell him what Christ did when you were the one who drifted. You are the hand on the rope. The Shepherd is the One who carries him in.

title: A Man Like Us
subtitle: from dust to the brother brought home
keyVerse: Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back, let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.

passage.text: Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. Is any cheerful? Let him sing praises.
Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord,

Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it didn’t rain on the earth for three years and six months.
He prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE PRAYING BROTHER
stationsIntro: Five words close the letter — words for the sick bed, the healing, the man like you, the wanderer, and the sins covered. Read each verse slowly, answer the question without dressing it up, and let the Greek drive you back into the verse.
lifeIntro: You have already been brought home. The Shepherd came after you, and Christ prays for you now. Out of that, James hands you five things to do this week — pray, call, confess, ask big, and go after the one who drifted — and none of them earns a thing.
lifePulls: You were the wanderer once. The Shepherd came after you, carried you home, and covered your sins with His own blood. Now He sends you down the same road after a brother.
prayer: Father, thank You for hearing the prayers of men made of dust. Thank You that the Lord Jesus lives to pray for me, even on the days I do not pray. When I suffer, turn my face to You; when I am glad, put a song in my mouth. When I am sick, give me the humility to call for help, and raise me up as You will. Give me a brother I can confess to, and make me a man he can confess to. You heard Elijah; hear me, and do not let me pray small. Send me after the man who has wandered, and use my voice to bring him home. Cover our sins with the blood of Christ, and keep us in Your truth until He comes. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, thank You for hearing the prayers of men made of dust.
Thank You that the Lord Jesus lives to pray for me, even on the days I do not pray.
When I suffer, turn my face to You; when I am glad, put a song in my mouth.
When I am sick, give me the humility to call for help, and raise me up as You will.
Give me a brother I can confess to, and make me a man he can confess to.
You heard Elijah; hear me, and do not let me pray small.
Send me after the man who has wandered, and use my voice to bring him home.
Cover our sins with the blood of Christ, and keep us in Your truth until He comes.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: James ends where a man needs him most: at the sickbed, in the confession, on his knees, and on the road after a brother. Pray in trouble and in joy. Call the elders. Confess your sins to one another. Elijah was made of your dust, and God heard him. The wanderer is worth the drive. His sins are covered by Christ’s blood, not your effort. Go anyway, because the Shepherd came for you.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see who stands around your bed. The Father is near, who gives to all liberally and without reproach. The Son is near, praying for you at the Father’s right hand. The elders are near, coming up the walk with oil in their hands and the name of the Lord on their lips. The brother you told the truth to is near. And the Lord who is coming is nearer than all of them, and He will raise up every one of His own from every bed and every grave.

Look back over the road James has walked you down. He met you in the trial and told you it was working endurance into you. He planted the word in you, the word which is able to save your souls. He showed you a faith with breath in it, and a tongue no man can tame brought under Christ’s hand. He held out the wisdom from above, pure and full of mercy. When your pride had run the field to ruin, he told you he gives more grace. When the waiting got long, he told you the Lord was at the door. Every command in this letter stood on a gift.

Now he sends you out with bent knees and open hands. You do not have to be Elijah’s better. Elijah sat under a juniper tree and asked to die, and God fed him and sent him back to work. He will not leave you under yours. The God who sent rain on Carmel still hears a man of dust. The blood that covered your sins still covers a multitude. And the Shepherd who came down the mountain looking for you still goes after the ones who wander, and He takes His brothers with Him. So pray when it hurts and sing when it does not. Call for the elders. Tell your brother the truth. Go and get the man who drifted. Then rest your whole weight on this: Jesus Christ bore your sins in His body on the tree, rose from the grave, and lives forever to intercede for you. Not one sin He covered will be uncovered. On the last day He will raise you up whole, and every wanderer He has carried home will be home for good. The brother you go after this week is going home to that same Lord.
closingVerse: Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back, let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
carry: Whose name came to mind when James spoke of the man who wanders from the truth, and what is keeping you from going after him the way Christ came after you?
